ACCESSIBILITY STATEMENT FOR SHOPEASY
================================================================================

Last updated: 16 May 2026
Audit date: 15 March 2024

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. INTRODUCTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ShopEasy is committed to ensuring digital accessibility for people with
disabilities. We continually improve the user experience for everyone and apply
relevant accessibility standards to achieve this goal.

This accessibility statement applies to the ShopEasy website and all web-based
services operated under the shopeasy.com domain (hereinafter "the Website").

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. CONFORMANCE STATUS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) define requirements for
designers and developers to improve accessibility for people with disabilities.
WCAG 2.1 defines three levels of conformance: Level A (minimum), Level AA
(enhanced), and Level AAA (highest). ShopEasy targets WCAG 2.1 Level AA
conformance.

CONFORMANCE CLAIM: ShopEasy PARTIALLY CONFORMS with WCAG 2.1 Level AA.

"Partially conforms" means that some parts of the content do not conform to
the accessibility standard. The specific non-conformances are identified in
Section 4 of this statement.

This conformance claim covers the ShopEasy website as a whole, including:
  - All product listing and detail pages
  - Shopping cart and checkout processes
  - Account registration and management
  - Search functionality
  - Customer support pages
  - Blog and editorial content
  - Embedded third-party widgets (where applicable)

Excluded from this claim:
  - Third-party content not under our direct control (e.g., external payment
    provider interfaces), where those providers maintain their own separate
    conformance claims.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ShopEasy relies on the following technologies for conformance with WCAG 2.1:

  - HTML5
  - CSS3
  - JavaScript (ECMAScript 2015+)
  - WAI-ARIA 1.1
  - PDF (Adobe PDF format; see known limitations in Section 4)

The Website has been tested with the following assistive technologies:

  - NVDA (NonVisual Desktop Access) with Mozilla Firefox on Windows
  - VoiceOver with Safari on macOS and iOS
  - Keyboard-only navigation (no pointing device)
  - Browser zoom up to 400%
  - Windows High Contrast Mode

Testing methodology: Combined automated scanning and manual testing.
  - Automated tools: [Specify tools used, e.g., axe-core, Deque Axe DevTools,
    Lighthouse Accessibility]
  - Manual testing conducted with the assistive technologies listed above.

Date of last comprehensive accessibility audit: 15 March 2024.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. KNOWN ACCESSIBILITY ISSUES (NON-CONFORMANCES)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The following known issues represent areas where ShopEasy does not currently
meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA. We are actively working to resolve these.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Issue 1: Inaccessible PDF Product Manuals
----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Affected content:
    Older PDF product manuals available for download on product detail pages.

  WCAG Success Criteria not met:
    - SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A): Some PDF documents contain images,
      diagrams, and non-text elements that lack appropriate text alternatives.
      Users relying on screen readers may not receive equivalent information.
    - SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A): Some older PDFs lack proper tag
      structure, form field labels, and programmatic attributes required for
      assistive technologies to interpret interactive elements and reading order
      correctly.

  Impact:
    Users who rely on screen readers or other assistive technologies may be
    unable to access the full content of affected PDF manuals.

  Accessible alternative:
    If you require an accessible version of a specific product manual, please
    contact our accessibility support team (see Section 6). We will provide an
    accessible alternative in HTML or plain-text format within 5 business days.

  Remediation plan:
    We are systematically remediating all product manuals. New manuals published
    after 1 January 2025 are produced to WCAG 2.1 AA standards. Remediation of
    legacy documents is ongoing, with an estimated completion date of
    [INSERT TARGET DATE].

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Issue 2: Live Chat Widget Does Not Announce New Messages
----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Affected content:
    The live chat widget available site-wide via the chat icon in the lower
    right corner of the screen.

  WCAG Success Criteria not met:
    - SC 4.1.3 Status Messages (Level AA): When a new chat message arrives from
      a support agent, the message is displayed visually but not communicated
      to screen reader users via an appropriate ARIA live region or equivalent
      programmatic mechanism. Users of screen readers may therefore miss
      incoming messages without switching focus manually to the chat panel.

  Impact:
    Screen reader users who initiate a live chat session may not be aware that
    a support agent has responded, resulting in a degraded or unusable support
    experience.

  Accessible alternative:
    Screen reader users who experience difficulty with the live chat widget are
    encouraged to contact our support team by email or telephone instead
    (see Section 6).

  Remediation plan:
    We are working with our live chat widget provider to implement ARIA live
    region announcements (role="log" or aria-live="polite") for incoming
    messages. This fix is targeted for completion by [INSERT TARGET DATE].

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Issue 3: Video Product Demonstrations Lack Audio Descriptions
----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Affected content:
    Embedded product demonstration videos on product detail pages and in the
    ShopEasy Learning Hub.

  WCAG Success Criteria not met:
    - SC 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded) (Level AA): Video product
      demonstrations contain visual information (e.g., on-screen text, product
      features shown only visually, button interactions) that is not conveyed
      through the existing audio track. Extended or inserted audio descriptions
      are not currently provided for any prerecorded video content.

  Impact:
    Users who are blind or have low vision and cannot perceive the visual
    content of product videos may be unable to obtain equivalent information
    about product features and usage.

  Accessible alternative:
    We are preparing text transcripts for all product demonstration videos.
    Where transcripts are currently available, they are linked directly below
    the video player. If no transcript is yet available for a specific video,
    please contact us (see Section 6) and we will provide a descriptive
    transcript within 5 business days.

  Remediation plan:
    Audio descriptions are being produced for all new product videos (effective
    immediately). Existing video library remediation is in progress, prioritised
    by product popularity, with an estimated completion date of
    [INSERT TARGET DATE].

Accessibility Statement for ShopEasy
=====================================

Last Updated: May 16, 2026


Our Commitment
--------------

ShopEasy is committed to ensuring digital accessibility for people with disabilities. We continually improve the user experience for everyone and apply relevant accessibility standards to ensure we provide an inclusive shopping experience.


Conformance Status
------------------

ShopEasy aims to conform to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 Level AA. These guidelines explain how to make web content more accessible to people with disabilities. Conformance with these guidelines helps make the web more user-friendly for all people.

We are partially conformant with WCAG 2.1 Level AA. "Partially conformant" means that some parts of the content do not fully conform to the accessibility standard due to the known issues listed below.


Known Accessibility Issues
--------------------------

We are aware of the following accessibility limitations on our website and are actively working to resolve them:

1. Older PDF Product Manuals (WCAG 2.1 SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content; SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value)
   Some of our older PDF product manuals were created before our current accessibility standards were adopted. These documents may not include proper alternative text for images and may not have correctly identified form fields, interactive elements, or structural markup. We are in the process of remediating these documents. In the meantime, if you need an accessible version of a product manual, please contact us and we will provide the information in an alternative format.

2. Live Chat Widget (WCAG 2.1 SC 4.1.3 Status Messages)
   Our live chat widget does not currently announce new incoming messages to users of screen readers. As a result, screen reader users may not be aware when a new chat message arrives without manually navigating to the chat area. We are working with our live chat provider to implement the necessary ARIA live region announcements. If you need assistance while we resolve this issue, please use our email or phone support options.

3. Video Product Demonstrations (WCAG 2.1 SC 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded))
   Product demonstration videos on our website do not currently include audio descriptions of the visual content shown. This means users who are blind or have low vision may miss visual information presented in the videos. We are in the process of producing audio description tracks for all product demonstration videos. If you need information about a product shown in a video, please contact us and we will assist you.


Technical Specifications
------------------------

ShopEasy relies on the following technologies for conformance with WCAG 2.1:

- HTML5
- CSS
- JavaScript
- WAI-ARIA


Audit and Assessment Approach
------------------------------

ShopEasy assesses the accessibility of our website through the following methods:

- Automated accessibility testing tools
- Manual testing with screen readers, including NVDA (Windows) and VoiceOver (macOS/iOS)
- Periodic expert reviews

Our most recent accessibility audit was conducted on March 15, 2024.


Feedback and Contact Information
----------------------------------

We welcome your feedback on the accessibility of ShopEasy. If you experience accessibility barriers on our website, or if you need information or a service in an accessible format, please contact us:

- Email: accessibility@shopeasy.com
- Phone: [Your Phone Number]
- Postal Address: [Your Company Address]

We aim to respond to accessibility feedback within 2 business days.


Formal Complaints
-----------------

If you are not satisfied with our response to your accessibility feedback, you may contact the relevant national authority responsible for enforcing accessibility regulations in your region.

# NZISM Certification & Accreditation Gap Analysis — RESTRICTED System

The NZISM is issued by the **GCSB (National Cyber Security Centre — NCSC NZ)** as the New Zealand Government's mandatory information security manual. Its controls carry **MUST/SHOULD compliance requirements tied to the system's classification level** — for a RESTRICTED system, essential (MUST) controls cannot be waived without formal risk acceptance recorded by the Accreditation Authority. Certification and Accreditation (C&A) is mandatory for any system handling Restricted and above before it goes live.

## What the NZISM C&A Process Requires

C&A has two distinct stages that must not be conflated:

- **Certification** — the technical assessment confirming NZISM controls are implemented *and effective*. This requires independent validation/testing evidence, not just documentation.
- **Accreditation** — the formal acceptance of residual risk by the Accreditation Authority (typically the agency head or a delegate), granting Authorisation to Operate (ATO).

The full pathway:

1. **System Security Plan (SSP/SecPlan)** — documents the system boundary, classification, security objectives, and all implemented controls.
2. **Security Risk Management Plan (SRMP)** — identifies threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, impact, treatments, and residual risk. This is a **mandatory** C&A artefact alongside the SSP, not optional.
3. **Control validation** — independent technical review verifying controls are implemented and effective (testing evidence required).
4. **Certification review and sign-off** — the ITSM (IT Security Manager) and CISO review validation evidence and formally certify the system.
5. **Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M)** — documents and tracks remediation of any assessment findings.
6. **Accreditation decision** — the Accreditation Authority reviews residual risk and grants ATO, recorded formally.
7. **Ongoing monitoring** — continuous control monitoring and periodic re-certification (typically every 1–3 years depending on risk, or triggered earlier by major change, incident, or classification change).

## Gap Analysis

| Item | NZISM Requirement | Your Status | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| System Security Plan | Mandatory C&A artefact; documents boundary, classification, objectives, controls | Draft exists | 🟡 Partial — confirm it covers full system boundary and all implemented/planned controls before certification review |
| Security Risk Management Plan | Mandatory C&A artefact (threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, impact, treatments, residual risk) | Does not exist | ❌ Not Implemented — **critical gap**; certification cannot proceed without an SRMP |
| Control implementation | Controls must be implemented and validated as effective for the classification level | Partially implemented | 🟡 Partial — identify which of the Restricted-tier control domains (physical secure zones, encryption at rest, MFA for remote access, privileged account separation, enhanced logging/12-month retention, supplier contractual controls, cloud risk assessment if applicable, MDM/remote wipe if mobile) remain outstanding |
| Control validation/testing | Independent technical testing evidence required — documentation alone is insufficient | No validation testing performed | ❌ Not Implemented — **critical gap**; even fully implemented controls cannot be certified without test evidence |
| Certification review and sign-off | ITSM/security practitioner and CISO review validation evidence and certify | Not started (no ITSM sign-off) | ❌ Not Implemented — blocked by the SRMP and validation gaps above |
| POA&M | Required to track remediation of certification findings | Not yet applicable (no certification run) | N/A pending certification |
| Accreditation decision | Accreditation Authority formally accepts residual risk and grants ATO | Not started | ❌ Not Implemented — cannot occur until certification is complete |

## Summary of Critical Gaps

Your agency currently cannot proceed to certification, let alone accreditation, for three interlocking reasons:

1. **No SRMP.** This is a mandatory artefact, not a nice-to-have. Without it, residual risk cannot be identified or presented to the Accreditation Authority.
2. **No control validation testing.** Partial implementation without testing evidence means the ITSM/CISO have nothing independently verifiable to certify against.
3. **No ITSM sign-off**, which is a direct consequence of gaps 1 and 2 — certification review cannot occur until the SRMP exists and validation testing has been completed.

## Recommended Remediation Priority

1. **Immediately**: Commission the SRMP — threat/vulnerability identification, likelihood/impact assessment, proposed treatments, and residual risk statement, scoped to the RESTRICTED classification.
2. **In parallel**: Complete implementation of outstanding Restricted-tier controls (encryption at rest, MFA for remote access, privileged access separation, enhanced logging with 12-month retention, physical secure zone controls, supplier contractual NZISM-equivalent clauses).
3. **Next**: Commission independent control validation/testing against the SSP and NZISM control set — this produces the evidence the ITSM/CISO need.
4. **Then**: ITSM and CISO conduct certification review, sign off, and raise a POA&M for any residual findings.
5. **Finally**: Submit the certification package (SSP, SRMP, validation evidence, POA&M) to the Accreditation Authority for the formal accreditation decision and ATO.

Given the current state (draft SSP, no SRMP, no validation testing, no ITSM sign-off), expect roughly 8–12+ weeks to reach an accreditation-ready position, depending on remediation effort for outstanding controls.

# NZISM Certification & Accreditation (C&A) Gap Analysis

## What the NZISM C&A Process Requires

Under the New Zealand Information Security Manual (NZISM), Certification and Accreditation is the formal process by which a system is assessed against its security requirements (certification) and then a risk-based decision is made by the appropriate authority to allow the system to operate (accreditation). For a RESTRICTED system, the process typically involves the following stages and artefacts:

1. **System Security Plan (SSP)** — Documents the system's architecture, boundary, security controls (mapped to NZISM chapters/controls), roles and responsibilities, and how the system meets its required security classification (RESTRICTED in this case).
2. **Security Risk Management Plan (SRMP)** — Captures the risk assessment for the system: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood/consequence ratings, existing and planned controls, residual risk, and risk treatment/acceptance decisions. The SRMP is the primary artefact used by the accreditation authority to understand and formally accept residual risk.
3. **Control implementation** — Controls identified in the SSP/SRMP as applicable (drawn from the NZISM control catalogue, e.g. access control, cryptography, network security, physical security, personnel security, incident management, system hardening) must actually be implemented, not merely planned.
4. **Security testing / validation** — Certification requires evidence that controls work as intended. This normally includes a combination of:
   - Vulnerability assessments
   - Penetration testing (where warranted by risk/classification)
   - Control validation / compliance testing against the SSP
   - Configuration and build reviews
5. **Certification** — A technical/independent review (often by an IT Security Manager, ITSM, or an independent certifier) confirms the system has been built and tested as described in the SSP and that residual risks are understood.
6. **Accreditation** — The system owner or Accreditation Authority (typically the Chief Executive or a delegate, informed by the Chief Information Security Officer / ITSM) formally accepts the residual risk and authorises the system to operate, usually issuing a time-bound accreditation with conditions and a re-accreditation/review date.
7. **Ongoing assurance** — Post-accreditation, the system requires continuous monitoring, periodic reassessment, vulnerability management, incident reporting, and re-accreditation on a defined cycle or upon significant change.

Key roles referenced in NZISM governance include the Chief Executive (ultimately accountable), the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), the IT Security Manager (ITSM) who manages day-to-day security and typically provides sign-off/advice into the accreditation decision, and system/business owners.

## Gap Analysis Against Your Current State

| C&A Requirement | Your Current State | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| System Security Plan | Draft exists | Not finalised/approved. Needs completion, internal review, and formal sign-off before it can support certification. |
| Security Risk Management Plan | Does not exist | **Critical gap.** Without an SRMP there is no documented risk assessment, no residual risk statement, and no basis for an accreditation decision. This should be prioritised immediately, in parallel with finalising the SSP. |
| Control implementation | Partially implemented | Gap between controls claimed in the SSP and controls actually operating. Need a control implementation matrix showing status (planned/in progress/implemented) for every applicable NZISM control, with target dates for full implementation. |
| Validation/compliance testing | None performed | **Critical gap.** No evidence controls work as intended. Certification cannot proceed without testing (vulnerability scanning at minimum, penetration testing if risk warrants given RESTRICTED classification). |
| Certification | Not started | Cannot occur until SSP is finalised, SRMP exists, controls are implemented, and testing evidence is available. |
| ITSM sign-off | Not obtained | **Critical gap.** No independent technical assurance has been given. ITSM sign-off (or equivalent independent certifier) is a precondition for accreditation. |
| Accreditation | Not obtained | Cannot be granted — accreditation authority has no SRMP, no test evidence, and no certification recommendation to base a decision on. The system should not be treated as authorised to hold/process RESTRICTED information until this is resolved. |

## Recommended Sequence to Close Gaps

1. Finalise the SSP, ensuring it maps every applicable NZISM control to the system and clearly defines the system boundary and classification handling requirements for RESTRICTED information.
2. Develop the SRMP in parallel — conduct a formal risk assessment (threat/vulnerability identification, likelihood/consequence, existing vs residual risk) and identify any additional controls or treatments required.
3. Complete implementation of all controls identified as applicable, tracking status in a control implementation/compliance matrix.
4. Commission validation testing — vulnerability assessment as a minimum, with penetration testing strongly recommended given the RESTRICTED classification — and remediate findings.
5. Package the SSP, SRMP, control evidence, and test results, and route through the ITSM (or independent certifier) for a formal certification recommendation.
6. Present the certification package to the Accreditation Authority (Chief Executive or delegate) for a risk-acceptance decision and formal accreditation, including any conditions and the re-accreditation timeframe.
7. Establish continuous monitoring and a defined re-accreditation/review cycle once accredited.

## Bottom Line

The agency currently has none of the three preconditions for accreditation of a RESTRICTED system: a finalised risk plan, tested/validated controls, and independent (ITSM) sign-off. Until the SRMP is produced, controls are fully implemented and validated through testing, and ITSM sign-off is obtained, the system should not be represented as certified or accredited to handle RESTRICTED information, and should not go into production processing RESTRICTED data without a documented and accepted interim risk position from the Accreditation Authority.

*This is general guidance based on NZISM C&A principles and does not replace consultation with your agency's CISO/ITSM or GCSB/NCSC advice for your specific system.*

# Hosting RESTRICTED Data in AWS Sydney (Offshore) — NZISM Requirements

The NZISM is issued by the **GCSB (National Cyber Security Centre — NCSC NZ)** as the New Zealand Government's mandatory information security manual. Its controls carry **MUST/SHOULD compliance requirements tied to the system's classification level**; for RESTRICTED data, essential (MUST) controls cannot be waived without formal risk acceptance by the Accreditation Authority.

**Short answer: yes, this is possible, but it is a risk-based decision, not a default option — offshore hosting of RESTRICTED data is not prohibited outright, but it requires a documented risk assessment and formal approval before go-live.** It is not something you can do simply because AWS Sydney is a reputable, capable region.

## The Required Pathway

### 1. Classify the data
Confirm the data is RESTRICTED (not higher) — this determines the applicable NZISM controls and the depth of assessment required. If any data processed by the system rises above RESTRICTED, offshore hosting becomes substantially harder to justify (Confidential+ generally requires Accrediting Authority approval for any offshore processing, per NZISM Chapter 13 supplier controls).

### 2. Run the NZ Government cloud risk assessment
The cloud-first policy requires a documented cloud risk assessment for public cloud use, per the **NZ Government Cloud Computing Risk & Resilience Guide**. **Protective Security Requirements (PSR)** obligations apply alongside the NZISM — the NZISM sits under the PSR for information security specifically, so both frameworks' cloud/offshore requirements must be satisfied.

### 3. Assess jurisdiction and sovereignty
Hosting in AWS Sydney places your data under **Australian legal jurisdiction**, not just AWS's operational control. You need to analyse:
- Foreign legal access regimes that could compel Amazon Web Services (or Australian authorities) to access or produce the data
- Data residency and data-in-transit commitments from AWS for the Sydney region
- Contractual protections limiting AWS's/subcontractors' ability to move or access data outside the agreed jurisdiction
- An exit strategy — data portability and secure deletion if the arrangement ends or needs to be unwound

### 4. Impose classification-appropriate controls
For RESTRICTED data hosted offshore, at minimum:
- **Encryption at rest and in transit**, with **agency-controlled keys where feasible** (evaluate AWS KMS with customer-managed keys, or an agency-held HSM-backed key model)
- **Access restricted to security-cleared personnel** only
- **Comprehensive logging and monitoring available to the agency** — not just to AWS; the agency must retain visibility (CloudTrail, VPC flow logs, config change logs exported to agency-controlled tooling)
- **Independent supplier assurance evidence** — an IRAP assessment of the AWS Sydney region/services in scope, current ISO/IEC 27001 certification, and a SOC 2 Type II report

### 5. Follow the approval chain and record it
This is not a decision an IT team can make alone:
1. Documented risk assessment (cloud risk assessment + jurisdiction/sovereignty analysis)
2. **ITSM/CISO certification review** of the assessment and proposed controls
3. **Formal risk acceptance by the Accreditation Authority / agency head** — recorded in the accreditation record — before go-live

Skipping the formal accreditation-record step is a common failure mode: agencies sometimes treat a positive risk assessment as sufficient, but the NZISM requires the Accreditation Authority to explicitly accept the residual risk of offshore hosting.

## Relevant Control References
Cloud computing controls sit in **NZISM Chapter 22 (Enterprise Systems Security), Section 22.1 Cloud Computing**, including control **22.1.23.C.01 (System availability)**. For topics beyond this verified control (e.g., specific offshore data-residency or key-management control numbers), confirm the current control ID against the online manual (nzism.gcsb.govt.nz) — the NZISM is updated roughly twice a year.

## Practical Recommendation
Before committing to AWS Sydney:
- Confirm whether an NZ-hosted alternative exists that would avoid the jurisdictional analysis entirely (data residency in NZ is generally preferred where available)
- If Sydney is the only viable option (e.g., service/feature parity, cost, or NZ region unavailable for the required AWS service), ensure the IRAP assessment, encryption/key-management model, and logging access are locked into the contract *before* the Accreditation Authority sign-off, not treated as follow-up items after go-live
- Document the decision, including why NZ hosting was not selected, in the accreditation record — this is what an auditor or the Accreditation Authority's successor will look for later

---

# Hosting RESTRICTED Data in AWS Sydney (Offshore): What's Required

## Short Answer

It is potentially possible, but **not automatic** — offshoring RESTRICTED information outside New Zealand requires a formal risk assessment, explicit risk acceptance by your agency's Accreditation Authority, and compliance with both the NZISM's offshore/cloud provisions and NZ Government cloud policy (administered by the Government Chief Digital Officer, GCDO, part of the Department of Internal Affairs). It is not a blanket prohibition, but it is treated as a heightened-risk decision that must be actively assessed and approved — you cannot simply provision an AWS Sydney region and start processing RESTRICTED data.

## What the NZISM Requires

1. **Data sovereignty and offshore risk assessment** — The NZISM requires agencies to consider the risks of storing or processing classified information offshore, including the jurisdiction's legal environment (e.g. foreign government access/compulsion laws), the physical and personnel security of the facility, and the ability to maintain NZ government assurance/audit rights over the environment.
2. **Classification-based controls** — RESTRICTED is the lowest NZ government security classification tier but still requires baseline protections: encryption of data at rest and in transit, strict access control, logging/monitoring, and personnel security (appropriately cleared/vetted administrators).
3. **Cloud-specific guidance** — The NZISM includes principles for cloud computing covering shared responsibility, provider assurance, data location, incident response coordination with the provider, and exit/portability planning. Agencies must satisfy themselves the cloud service provider (CSP) can meet the confidentiality, integrity, and availability requirements of the classification level.
4. **Certification and accreditation** — As with any system handling RESTRICTED information, the hosting arrangement (including the offshore element) must be captured in the System Security Plan and Security Risk Management Plan, and the residual risk of offshoring must be explicitly accepted by the agency's Accreditation Authority (typically Chief Executive or delegate, informed by the CISO/ITSM).

## What NZ Government Cloud Policy Requires

1. **Cloud First Policy** — NZ government's Cloud First policy encourages use of cloud services but requires agencies to conduct due diligence, particularly for higher-sensitivity data.
2. **Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO) guidance** — The GCDO (within DIA) provides guidance and, historically, a Cloud Risk Assessment process/tooling to help agencies assess cloud service risk, including data sovereignty, jurisdiction, and provider security certifications. Agencies are generally expected to consult this guidance before onboarding a cloud service for anything above UNCLASSIFIED, and certainly for RESTRICTED.
3. **All-of-Government (AoG) cloud arrangements** — Where an AoG cloud services agreement exists covering a provider (AWS has historically had engagement under NZ government cloud frameworks), agencies should check whether AWS Sydney is an approved/endorsed offering under that arrangement, as this can streamline (but not eliminate) the due diligence and approval steps.
4. **Data sovereignty considerations** — Even though AWS Sydney is in Australia (not New Zealand), it is still an offshore location relative to NZ. Agencies must specifically assess and document why an NZ-only region isn't used (AWS has historically not had a dedicated NZ region for all services, so many agencies do host in Australian regions), the legal exposure of data being subject to Australian law and any third-country access risk, and any restrictions from data owners or information-sharing agreements that may prohibit offshoring entirely for certain data sets.
5. **Ministerial/Cabinet direction** — Certain categories of government data (e.g. specific national security, law enforcement, or Māori data considerations) may have additional sovereignty requirements or expectations beyond general RESTRICTED handling — these should be checked against your specific data holdings.

## Practical Pre-Conditions Before Hosting RESTRICTED Data in AWS Sydney

- Conduct a documented risk assessment covering data sovereignty, legal jurisdiction (Australian and any extraterritorial access laws such as the US CLOUD Act, given AWS is a US-headquartered provider), and provider security assurance (e.g. relevant certifications, NZISM control mapping).
- Confirm AWS's shared responsibility model and ensure your agency retains/implements the customer-side NZISM controls (encryption key management, IAM, logging, network segmentation, etc.).
- Verify whether AWS Sydney is covered by any existing NZ Government cloud services arrangement or requires a standalone risk assessment submission to GCDO/DIA.
- Ensure contractual terms with AWS address data location commitments, government/law enforcement access notification, audit rights, incident notification timeframes, and data return/deletion on exit.
- Document the offshoring decision and residual risk in the SRMP and obtain explicit accreditation sign-off before go-live, rather than treating cloud hosting as a lower-scrutiny "given."
- Engage your agency's CISO/ITSM and, where relevant, NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCSB) for advice, particularly given RESTRICTED classification.

## Bottom Line

RESTRICTED data can potentially be hosted in AWS Sydney, but this is a risk-accepted exception rather than a default — it requires a documented offshore risk assessment, alignment with GCDO/NZ Government cloud policy expectations, explicit customer-side implementation of NZISM controls under the shared responsibility model, and formal accreditation sign-off before the data is placed there. Treat this as a decision requiring active governance, not a routine provisioning task.

# Access Control Policy

**Classification:** IN-CONFIDENCE (policy document itself; apply the classification marking of the agency issuing this policy)
**Framework:** New Zealand Information Security Manual (NZISM)

The NZISM is issued by the **GCSB (National Cyber Security Centre — NCSC NZ)** as the New Zealand Government's mandatory information security manual. Its controls carry **MUST/SHOULD compliance requirements tied to the system's classification level** — essential (MUST) controls in this policy cannot be waived for systems handling Restricted information or above without formal risk acceptance by the Accreditation Authority. This policy is written to be applicable at the RESTRICTED tier by default; agencies operating solely at IN-CONFIDENCE or below may descope the Restricted-tier requirements noted below.

---

## 1. Purpose

This Access Control Policy establishes the requirements for identification, authentication, authorisation, and privileged access management across all agency information systems, in accordance with the NZISM. It ensures access to agency information and systems is limited to authorised individuals with a legitimate business need.

## 2. Scope

This policy applies to all agency employees, contractors, and third parties who access agency ICT systems, and to all systems processing agency information from Unclassified through Restricted (and above, where the agency operates such systems, subject to the additional controls in NZISM Chapters for Confidential/Secret/Top Secret).

## 3. Policy Statements

### 3.1 Identification
- Every user, service, and device accessing an agency system must be uniquely identified. Shared or generic accounts are prohibited except where formally risk-assessed and approved, with compensating controls (e.g., session recording).
- Service accounts must use unique, non-shared credentials and be inventoried with a named business owner.
- *NZISM reference: Chapter 16.1, Identification, Authentication and Passwords — confirm current control numbers against the online manual for identification-specific requirements beyond those cited below.*

### 3.2 Authentication
- Passwords must meet complexity and minimum-length requirements aligned with NZISM guidance (which follows NIST SP 800-63B principles).
- **Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) is mandatory** for all remote access and for all privileged accounts, and is required for all users accessing Restricted information.
- Account lockout must be enforced after a defined number of failed login attempts.
- Session timeout and automatic screen lock must be configured on all endpoints accessing agency systems.
- Inactive or departed-staff accounts must be suspended promptly.
- *NZISM reference: 16.1.46.C.02 (Suspension of access — disable inactive/departed accounts), and Chapter 16.1 generally for MFA and password requirements. Confirm current v3.9 control numbers for passwordless/phishing-resistant MFA requirements against the online manual, as the NZISM is updated roughly twice a year.*

### 3.3 Authorisation
- Access is granted strictly on the **principle of least privilege** — the minimum access necessary for the individual's role.
- **Separation of duties** must be enforced for critical or high-risk functions (e.g., no single individual can both create and approve a privileged account).
- Access rights must be reviewed and re-certified **at least annually**, with more frequent review for privileged and Restricted-tier access.
- Temporary or time-limited access must be formally requested, approved, and configured to expire automatically.
- Access requests, approvals, and revocations must be logged and auditable.
- *NZISM reference: Chapter 16 (Access Control and Passwords / v3.9: Authentication and Access Controls) generally for least privilege and access review requirements — confirm current control numbers for specific authorisation sub-controls against the online manual.*

### 3.4 Privileged Access
- Privileged accounts must be **separate from standard user accounts** — no individual should use a privileged account for routine business activity (email, web browsing, document editing).
- Privileged access is granted on a need-to-use basis and subject to enhanced approval.
- All privileged account activity must be logged, and logs reviewed periodically for anomalous use.
- Remote privileged access requires additional controls — jump servers and, where the system handles Restricted+ information, session recording.
- Privileged accounts must be included in the mandatory annual access review, with more frequent review recommended (e.g., quarterly).
- *NZISM reference: 16.3.5.C.02 (Use of privileged accounts — restrict, separate, least privilege).*

### 3.5 Access Logging and Monitoring
- All authentication events (successful and failed logins), privileged actions, and access changes must be logged.
- Logs must be protected against tampering and retained per NZISM requirements (minimum 90 days online, 12 months archived for Restricted-tier systems; longer for Confidential and above).
- *NZISM reference: 16.6.6.C.02 (Maintaining system management logs), 16.6.10.C.02 (Additional events to be logged).*

## 4. Roles and Responsibilities
- **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO):** owns this policy, approves exceptions, reviews compliance annually.
- **System/Application Owners:** ensure access controls are implemented and reviewed for their systems.
- **IT Security Manager (ITSM):** validates access control implementation as part of certification activities.
- **Line Managers:** approve and periodically review access requests for their staff.
- **All Users:** comply with authentication requirements and report suspected unauthorised access immediately.

## 5. Exceptions
Any exception to this policy (e.g., use of a shared account, deferral of MFA) requires documented risk assessment and formal approval by the CISO, and — for Restricted-tier systems — acknowledgement by the Accreditation Authority as part of the system's residual risk position.

## 6. Review Cycle
This policy must be reviewed **at least annually**, or earlier following a significant security incident, major system change, or update to the NZISM.

## 7. Document Control

# Access Control Policy

**[Agency Name]**
**Document Owner:** Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)
**Effective Date:** 3 July 2026
**Alignment:** New Zealand Information Security Manual (NZISM)
**Classification:** UNCLASSIFIED (Policy Document)

## 1. Purpose

This policy establishes the requirements for controlling access to [Agency Name]'s information systems and information, in alignment with the New Zealand Information Security Manual (NZISM). It ensures that access to systems and data is granted only to authorised individuals, based on identified business need, and is managed throughout the access lifecycle.

## 2. Scope

This policy applies to all employees, contractors, and third parties who access [Agency Name]'s systems, networks, applications, or information, at all classification levels handled by the agency (UNCLASSIFIED through RESTRICTED and above, as applicable).

## 3. Policy Statements

### 3.1 Identification

- All users must be uniquely identified before being granted access to agency systems. Shared or generic accounts are prohibited except where explicitly approved and compensating controls (e.g. enhanced logging, physical access restriction) are documented.
- User identities must be verified and formally registered as part of the onboarding process, consistent with NZISM personnel and identification requirements for account management.
- Unique identifiers must be maintained for the life of the account and not reused or reassigned to another individual.

*(Aligned to NZISM access control / identification and authentication chapter requirements.)*

### 3.2 Authentication

- Access to all agency systems must be authenticated using mechanisms appropriate to the classification of information involved. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required for:
  - Remote access to agency networks and systems
  - Access to systems processing RESTRICTED or higher classified information
  - All privileged/administrative accounts
- Passwords/passphrases, where used as a factor, must meet minimum complexity, length, and rotation requirements consistent with NZISM password guidance, and must not be shared, written down insecurely, or reused across systems.
- Authentication credentials must be securely stored (e.g. salted/hashed) and transmitted only over encrypted channels.
- Default vendor credentials must be changed or disabled prior to system deployment.

*(Aligned to NZISM authentication controls, including multi-factor authentication requirements for remote and privileged access.)*

### 3.3 Authorisation

- Access to systems and information must be granted according to the principle of least privilege — users are given the minimum access necessary to perform their duties.
- Access must be formally requested, approved by the relevant information/system owner, and recorded prior to provisioning.
- Role-based access control (RBAC) should be used where practicable to standardise permissions according to job function.
- Access rights must be reviewed at least annually, and immediately upon role change or termination, to ensure continued business need (access recertification).
- Segregation of duties must be enforced for sensitive functions (e.g. system administration, financial approval, security configuration) to reduce the risk of fraud or error.
- Access to information classified RESTRICTED or above additionally requires the user to hold an appropriate security clearance and need-to-know, consistent with NZISM personnel security and information classification handling requirements.

*(Aligned to NZISM authorisation and account management controls, including least privilege, need-to-know, and periodic access review requirements.)*

### 3.4 Privileged Access Management

- Privileged accounts (system administrators, database administrators, security administrators, and similar) must be:
  - Separate from standard user accounts (no use of privileged accounts for routine business activities such as email or web browsing)
  - Individually attributable — no shared privileged accounts
  - Subject to MFA for all access
  - Approved by the system/business owner and CISO (or delegate) prior to provisioning
  - Logged and monitored, with privileged session activity subject to enhanced audit logging
  - Reviewed at a higher frequency than standard accounts (e.g. quarterly) due to elevated risk
- Use of privileged access must be time-bound and task-justified where practicable (e.g. just-in-time access, break-glass procedures with post-use review for emergency access).
- Remote privileged access must be via secure, authenticated, and encrypted channels, with additional monitoring controls.
- All privileged account activity must be logged in a manner that is protected from modification or deletion by the account holder, supporting accountability and incident investigation.

*(Aligned to NZISM privileged access management and system administration control requirements.)*

## 4. Account Lifecycle Management

- **Provisioning:** Access is provisioned only after approval from the relevant owner and completion of required pre-employment/security screening appropriate to the classification of data accessed.
- **Modification:** Access changes (e.g. role transfer) must be re-approved to reflect the new role's requirements; residual unnecessary access must be removed.
- **De-provisioning:** Access must be revoked immediately upon termination of employment/contract, and within a defined maximum timeframe (e.g. same business day) for role changes that remove the need for access.
- **Inactive accounts:** Accounts inactive for a defined period (e.g. 90 days) must be disabled and reviewed.

## 5. Monitoring and Audit

- All authentication and authorisation events, particularly privileged access and access to RESTRICTED information, must be logged.
- Logs must be protected from unauthorised access or modification and retained in accordance with agency record-keeping and NZISM logging/audit requirements.
- Access control logs should be reviewed periodically and investigated where anomalies are detected.

## 6. Roles and Responsibilities

- **System/Information Owners:** Approve access requests and conduct periodic access reviews for their systems/information.
- **CISO / IT Security Manager (ITSM):** Owns this policy, approves privileged access provisioning, and oversees compliance monitoring.
- **IT Operations:** Implements technical access controls, provisions/de-provisions accounts, and maintains audit logs.
- **All Staff and Contractors:** Comply with this policy, protect their credentials, and report suspected unauthorised access immediately.

## 7. Exceptions

Any exception to this policy must be documented, risk-assessed, and formally approved by the CISO, with compensating controls identified and a defined review/expiry date.

## 8. Review

This policy will be reviewed at least annually, or upon significant change to the agency's systems, threat environment, or the NZISM.

---

*This policy is drafted as a general template aligned to NZISM access control principles (identification, authentication, authorisation, and privileged access management). It should be reviewed and tailored by the agency's CISO/ITSM against the current NZISM version and the agency's specific systems, classification holdings, and risk profile before formal adoption.*

# Supplier Ransomware Incident — NZISM-Aligned Incident Response Obligations

The NZISM is issued by the **GCSB (National Cyber Security Centre — NCSC NZ)** as the New Zealand Government's mandatory information security manual. Its controls carry **MUST/SHOULD compliance requirements tied to the system's classification level** — for a supplier holding your agency's data, essential (MUST) obligations around incident reporting and supplier accountability apply regardless of where the breach originated, and cannot simply be waived because the compromise occurred at a third party.

**Critical point: your agency remains responsible for the security of its information even when a third-party supplier is holding it.** A ransomware event at your supplier is your incident too, not solely theirs.

## Immediate Steps

### 1. Activate your incident response plan
Treat this as a live agency security incident under your Incident Response Plan, not merely a "vendor problem to monitor." Classify severity based on: the classification level of the data held by the supplier, whether personal information is involved, and whether the ransomware event involved data exfiltration (not just encryption/denial of access).

### 2. Engage the supplier under contract
- Invoke incident notification and cooperation clauses in your supplier contract — the supplier should already be contractually obligated to notify you of breaches within a defined timeframe.
- Demand details: what data was affected, whether exfiltration occurred (not just encryption), the timeline of compromise, and the supplier's containment/eradication actions.
- Preserve evidence — request the supplier maintain forensic readiness and chain of custody for incident artefacts; do not let remediation destroy evidence needed for your own assessment.

### 3. Assess data and classification impact
Determine what classification of agency data the supplier held (Unclassified through Restricted or above) and whether personal information was involved. This determines both your NZISM reporting obligations and your Privacy Act 2020 obligations.

## Who You Must Notify in New Zealand

- **NCSC (GCSB)** — for cyber incidents. Report significant security incidents to the NCSC; note that **CERT NZ's functions now sit within the NCSC**, so there is a single agency to engage for both the "government cyber incident" reporting line and what was formerly the CERT NZ incident-reporting function. This applies whether the compromise happened on your own systems or, as here, at a supplier holding your data — the obligation follows the data, not just the infrastructure.
- **NZ Police** — for criminal acts. Ransomware is a criminal act (extortion/computer crime); report to NZ Police, particularly if there is a ransom demand or evidence of criminal exploitation.
- **Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC)** — if personal information is involved and the breach meets the **notifiable serious-harm threshold** under the Privacy Act 2020. This is a mandatory, time-bound obligation independent of your NZISM reporting — assess it in parallel, not after NCSC/Police notification is complete.

Do not treat these as sequential or optional — assess all three notification obligations in parallel as soon as the scope of affected data is known, even if the full picture is still emerging. Initial notifications can (and often should) be made with preliminary information, followed by updates as the investigation matures.

## Supplier and Contractual Obligations Going Forward

- **Right to audit**: exercise any contractual right to audit the supplier's security controls and incident response as part of this event.
- **Incident notification SLA**: confirm the supplier met their contractual notification timeframe; if they did not, this is itself a contract compliance issue to raise formally.
- **Post-incident review**: require the supplier to provide a root-cause analysis and remediation plan; your agency should conduct its own post-incident review covering both the supplier's failure and your own oversight of that supplier relationship.
- **Supplier risk register**: log this event against the supplier in your risk register, and reassess whether the existing risk acceptance for this supplier relationship still holds.
- **Reassess offshore/hosting arrangements**: if the supplier's compromised environment was hosting Restricted+ data, this event should trigger a re-review of the original risk assessment and the Accreditation Authority's residual risk acceptance for that arrangement (NZISM Chapter 13, Third-Party Suppliers).

## Documentation and Recertification Impact

- Maintain a full incident timeline, notifications made, and remediation actions taken.
- If the affected system underwent NZISM Certification & Accreditation, a significant security incident is a **re-certification trigger** — the ITSM/CISO should assess whether the system's certification remains valid or whether re-certification is required.
- Conduct a post-incident review with root-cause analysis and lessons learned, feeding into both your own control improvements and any renegotiation of the supplier contract's security clauses.

---
*This is general compliance guidance, not legal advice. Confirm current NCSC/CERT NZ reporting channels, Privacy Act 2020 notifiable-harm thresholds, and NZ Police reporting procedures against official sources, and consult legal counsel given the potential contractual, regulatory, and criminal dimensions of this incident.*

# Supplier Ransomware Incident: NZISM-Aligned Incident Response Obligations

## Immediate Situation

A supplier holding your agency's data has been hit by ransomware. This is a third-party/supply-chain security incident affecting your agency's information, and it triggers your agency's own incident response obligations under the NZISM even though the breach originated at the supplier, because the data compromised is your agency's information.

## Step 1: Activate Incident Response and Contain

- Activate your agency's incident response plan immediately, treating this as a confirmed (not suspected) security incident given ransomware has already executed at the supplier.
- Engage the supplier urgently to understand: what agency data was held, whether it was accessed/exfiltrated (not just encrypted), the classification level of the affected data, the timeline of compromise, and containment/eradication status.
- Assess whether the supplier's compromise creates any onward risk to your agency's own systems (e.g. shared credentials, VPN access, integrations, or API connections between the supplier and your environment) and isolate/rotate credentials as a precaution.
- Preserve evidence and maintain a timeline/incident log from the moment you are notified.

## Step 2: Classify the Incident and Determine Notification Obligations

Under NZISM, security incidents affecting government information must be assessed for severity and reported through appropriate channels. Key considerations:

1. **Assess data classification and sensitivity** — what classification was the compromised data (e.g. RESTRICTED, personal information, etc.)? This drives urgency and who must be notified.
2. **Determine whether this is a "reportable" security incident** under NZISM criteria — ransomware affecting a system holding government information, particularly with potential data exfiltration, would typically meet the threshold for mandatory reporting.

## Who You Must Notify in New Zealand

Depending on the nature and classification of the data and the type of information involved, notification obligations can include:

1. **National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)**, part of the **Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB)** — NZISM requires agencies to report significant cyber security incidents affecting government systems/information to NCSC. Ransomware incidents affecting a supplier holding government data should be reported to NCSC as the national technical authority for government cyber security incidents.
2. **CERT NZ** — for broader incident reporting/coordination, particularly if there is any consumer or wider public impact, or as a parallel reporting channel alongside NCSC (CERT NZ and NCSC coordinate on national incident response).
3. **Your agency's own CISO/ITSM and senior leadership/Chief Executive** — internal escalation is required immediately so the agency can make risk decisions (e.g. whether to suspend the supplier relationship, notify affected individuals, or issue public statements).
4. **Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC)** — if the compromised data includes personal information, and the breach has caused or is likely to cause serious harm, this is a **notifiable privacy breach** under the Privacy Act 2020, which requires notification to the Privacy Commissioner and affected individuals as soon as practicable.
5. **Affected individuals** — if personal information is compromised and serious harm is likely, individuals must be notified under the Privacy Act 2020 notifiable breach regime, in addition to the technical agency notifications above.
6. **Relevant Minister / Ministry** — for significant incidents, agencies typically need to brief their Minister and, where relevant, the lead central agency (e.g. Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet for national security-significant events), particularly if the incident could become public or affects multiple agencies.
7. **Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO) / Department of Internal Affairs** — where the incident relates to a cloud service or shared government ICT arrangement, GCDO may need to be informed as the functional lead for government digital services.

## Step 3: Supplier/Contractual Obligations

- Review your contract with the supplier for mandatory breach notification clauses, timeframes, cooperation obligations (forensic access, evidence sharing), and liability provisions.
- Require the supplier to provide a formal incident report, including root cause, data affected, and remediation actions.
- Assess whether the supplier met their contracted security obligations (this may be a separate compliance/contractual matter to pursue after the immediate incident is managed).

## Step 4: Investigation and Remediation

- Conduct or commission a forensic assessment (via the supplier or independently) to determine the scope of data compromise.
- Determine whether any of your agency's credentials, systems, or connected infrastructure were also exposed, and remediate (e.g. password resets, access revocation, network segmentation review).
- Document lessons learned and update supplier risk assessments/due diligence processes.

## Step 5: Post-Incident Reporting and Review

- Complete a formal incident report for internal governance, capturing timeline, impact, notifications made, and remediation actions.
- Feed findings into your agency's Security Risk Management Plan and supplier risk register — this incident should trigger a review of the supplier's ongoing suitability to hold agency data, and possibly a broader review of other suppliers with similar data holdings.
- Consider whether NZISM control gaps (e.g. contractual security requirements, data minimisation with suppliers, encryption of data at rest at the supplier) need strengthening agency-wide as a result.

## Summary of Key NZ Notification Contacts

- **NCSC (GCSB)** — national technical authority for significant government cyber incidents
- **CERT NZ** — national incident reporting/coordination body
- **Office of the Privacy Commissioner** — mandatory if personal information and serious harm likely (Privacy Act 2020)
- **Internal CISO/ITSM/Chief Executive** — immediate internal escalation
- **Affected individuals** — if personal information compromised with likely serious harm

## Bottom Line

Treat this as your agency's own reportable security incident, not solely the supplier's problem. Contain and assess immediately, notify NCSC (and CERT NZ) given this is a government-information-affecting cyber incident, assess Privacy Act notification obligations if personal information is involved, escalate internally to your CISO and Chief Executive, and enforce your contractual incident cooperation and notification clauses with the supplier. Document everything for both incident response and any subsequent supplier accountability review.

*This is general guidance based on NZISM incident management principles and NZ notification frameworks (NCSC, CERT NZ, Privacy Act 2020). Confirm exact reporting thresholds and timeframes with your agency's CISO/ITSM, as these depend on the specific classification and nature of the compromised data.*

# NZISM-Aligned Due Diligence for SaaS Procurement

The NZISM is issued by the **GCSB (National Cyber Security Centre — NCSC NZ)** as the New Zealand Government's mandatory information security manual. Its controls carry **MUST/SHOULD compliance requirements tied to the classification of the data the SaaS product will handle** — the higher the classification, the more rigorous the due diligence and the less negotiable the contractual requirements. **Your agency remains responsible for the security of its information even though the SaaS product is hosted and operated by a third party** — you cannot transfer that accountability to the vendor.

## Step 1: Classify the Data First

Before evaluating any vendor, determine the classification of the data the SaaS product will store or process (Unclassified through Restricted, or above). This determines the depth of assessment required and which contractual protections are mandatory versus best-practice. Default to treating the system as **Restricted** if this is not yet firmly established — it is easier to relax requirements later than to retrofit them after go-live.

## Step 2: Independent Assurance Evidence to Require

Before contract execution, obtain and review:
- **Current ISO/IEC 27001 certificate** — check the certificate scope actually covers the service, environment, and data centres relevant to your deployment, not just the vendor's corporate entity in general.
- **SOC 2 Type II report** — covering a sufficient audit period (12 months preferred), reviewed for exceptions and management responses.
- **IRAP assessment** (or equivalent government-grade assessment) — particularly important if the vendor is hosted on a public cloud platform and the data will reach Restricted classification.
- **Recent independent penetration test results**, including remediation status of any findings — do not accept a clean summary without visibility into what was tested and what remains open.

## Step 3: Architecture Evidence to Require

- **Tenancy isolation model** — confirm how your agency's data is logically/physically separated from other tenants.
- **Encryption at rest and in transit** — confirm approved algorithms (AES-256, TLS 1.2 minimum, TLS 1.3 preferred) are used throughout.
- **Key management** — clarify who holds encryption keys; for Restricted+ data, agency-controlled keys are preferred where feasible.
- **Data residency and processing locations** — identify every jurisdiction where your data will be stored, processed, or backed up, including any offshore processing.
- **Subcontractor/fourth-party disclosure** — the vendor must disclose all subcontractors and downstream processors with access to your data, since your due diligence obligations extend through the supply chain, not just the primary vendor.

## Step 4: Identity & Access Integration (Contractual Requirements, Not Nice-to-Haves)

- **SSO/SAML or OIDC support** — the SaaS product must integrate with your agency's identity provider; standalone credential stores are a red flag for Restricted-tier use.
- **MFA enforcement** — must be supported and enforceable for all users, non-negotiable for privileged/admin accounts.
- **Role-based access control (RBAC)** — granular enough to implement least privilege and separation of duties for your agency's use cases.
- **Agency access to audit logs** — export or API access to authentication events, privileged actions, and configuration changes; you cannot rely solely on the vendor's internal logging with no visibility for your own security monitoring.

## Step 5: Contract Clauses to Impose

- **Incident notification SLA** — a defined, short timeframe (e.g., 24–72 hours from vendor's own detection) for notifying your agency of any security incident affecting your data, including incidents at the vendor's subcontractors.
- **Right to audit** — contractual right to audit the vendor's security controls, or at minimum to receive current assurance evidence (ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, pen test summary) annually.
- **Data return and certified secure deletion on exit** — data portability in a usable format plus certified destruction of all copies (including backups) at contract termination, consistent with NZISM disposal requirements for the applicable classification.
- **Jurisdiction / data-sovereignty terms** — explicit statement of which jurisdictions' laws govern the data, and restrictions on moving data outside agreed locations without agency approval.

## Step 6: Offshore Hosting Considerations

If the SaaS product hosts data outside New Zealand (a common reality for global SaaS platforms), this is a **risk-based decision, not a prohibition**, but it requires:
1. A documented cloud/offshore risk assessment (NZ Government Cloud Computing Risk & Resilience Guide; Protective Security Requirements obligations apply alongside the NZISM).
2. Jurisdictional and legal-access-regime analysis for the hosting country.
3. Classification-appropriate controls (encryption with agency-influenced key management, cleared-personnel access, agency-visible logging, supplier assurance evidence as above).
4. **ITSM/CISO certification review**, followed by **formal risk acceptance by the Accreditation Authority / agency head** — recorded in the accreditation record — before go-live, if the data is Restricted or above.

## Step 7: Ongoing Assurance (Post-Contract)

- **Annual reassessment** of the vendor's security posture and updated assurance evidence.
- **Monitoring of vendor security advisories** and any disclosed incidents throughout the contract term.
- **Supplier risk register entry** — formally logged, reviewed, and updated as part of the agency's ongoing third-party risk management.
- **Formal risk acceptance for any residual gaps** — if the vendor cannot meet a specific requirement (e.g., no agency-controlled keys available), document the gap and obtain explicit risk acceptance from the appropriate authority rather than proceeding silently.

## Relevant NZISM References
Cloud/offshore hosting: **Chapter 22 (Enterprise Systems Security), Section 22.1 Cloud Computing**, including control **22.1.23.C.01 (System availability)**. Access control and privileged access integration requirements: **Chapter 16 (Access Control and Passwords / v3.9: Authentication and Access Controls)**, including **16.1.46.C.02** (account suspension) and **16.3.5.C.02** (privileged account use). Third-party supplier obligations generally: **Chapter 13, Third-Party Suppliers**. For control numbers not listed here, confirm the current citation against the online manual (nzism.gcsb.govt.nz), as the NZISM is updated roughly twice a year.

---
*This is general compliance guidance, not legal advice. Confirm current NZISM control numbering and PSR requirements against official sources, and have procurement/legal counsel review final contract language before execution.*

# NZISM-Aligned Due Diligence and Contractual Security Requirements for SaaS Procurement

## Purpose

When procuring a SaaS product for agency use, your agency remains accountable for the security of any government information processed by the vendor, even though the underlying infrastructure and application are managed by a third party. The following due diligence and contractual requirements are aligned to NZISM principles for outsourced/cloud service arrangements.

## 1. Pre-Procurement Due Diligence

### 1.1 Data Classification and Risk Assessment
- Determine the classification of data that will be stored/processed in the SaaS product (UNCLASSIFIED through RESTRICTED or higher). This drives the level of assurance required.
- Conduct a risk assessment covering confidentiality, integrity, and availability requirements for the data involved, and document it (feeding into your Security Risk Management Plan).
- Assess whether the SaaS product is fit for the classification level intended — some SaaS offerings may not be appropriate for RESTRICTED or higher information without additional controls.

### 1.2 Vendor Security Assurance
- Request evidence of the vendor's security posture: relevant independent certifications (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2 Type II), penetration testing results, and vulnerability management practices.
- Review the vendor's data centre/hosting arrangements, including sub-processors and where data is physically stored/processed (data sovereignty).
- Assess the vendor's incident history and any known past breaches.
- Where the SaaS product is offered via a hyperscaler (AWS, Azure, GCP, etc.), confirm the shared responsibility model — what security controls the vendor/platform provides versus what your agency must configure and manage.

### 1.3 Data Sovereignty and Offshoring
- Identify where data will be stored and processed, including backup/DR locations and any offshore sub-processors.
- If data will be held offshore, apply the same offshore risk assessment rigour as for any cloud hosting decision — legal jurisdiction risk, foreign government access laws, and NZ Government cloud policy expectations (via GCDO/DIA guidance).
- Confirm whether an All-of-Government (AoG) or existing government-negotiated arrangement covers this vendor, which may streamline (but not replace) due diligence.

### 1.4 Personnel and Supply Chain
- Assess vendor personnel security practices (background checks/vetting) for staff with administrative access to your data.
- Assess the vendor's own supply chain/sub-processor risk (fourth-party risk) — who else might touch your data.

## 2. Contractual Security Requirements to Impose

### 2.1 Data Handling and Classification
- Explicit contractual acknowledgement of the classification of data being processed and the corresponding handling obligations (aligned to NZISM classification handling requirements).
- Data minimisation — vendor must only collect/process data necessary for the service.
- Prohibition on secondary use of agency data (e.g. for vendor's own analytics, AI training, or marketing) without explicit written agency consent.

### 2.2 Security Controls
- Requirement for encryption of data at rest and in transit, using agency-acceptable standards.
- Requirement for strong access control on the vendor side — MFA, least privilege, logging of administrative access to agency data/tenancy.
- Right for the agency (or an independent auditor on the agency's behalf) to audit or request evidence of the vendor's compliance with these requirements periodically.
- Vulnerability and patch management obligations with defined remediation timeframes based on severity.

### 2.3 Data Location and Sovereignty
- Contractual commitment on data location (specific regions/data centres) and advance notification/agreement requirement before changing data location or adding new sub-processors.
- Restrictions or notification requirements regarding disclosure of agency data in response to foreign government/legal requests, to the extent achievable.

### 2.4 Incident Management
- Mandatory breach/incident notification clause with a defined maximum notification timeframe (e.g. within 24–72 hours of the vendor becoming aware) to the agency.
- Requirement for vendor cooperation in incident investigation, including provision of logs, forensic access, and root cause analysis.
- Clear escalation contacts and a joint incident response process, referencing your agency's obligation to report significant incidents to NCSC/CERT NZ and, where personal information is involved, the Privacy Act 2020 breach notification regime.

### 2.5 Business Continuity and Exit
- Defined service availability/continuity commitments (SLAs) appropriate to how critical the service is to agency operations.
- Data backup and disaster recovery commitments.
- Exit/termination clause guaranteeing return or secure destruction of agency data within a defined period, and data portability in a usable format, to avoid vendor lock-in and ensure a clean transition if the contract ends or the vendor is compromised.

### 2.6 Compliance and Audit Rights
- Right to audit (directly or via independent third party) the vendor's security controls, at least for higher-classification data or higher-risk services.
- Requirement for the vendor to promptly notify the agency of material changes to their security posture, ownership, sub-processors, or certifications.
- Flow-down clauses requiring the vendor's sub-processors to meet equivalent security obligations.

### 2.7 Personnel Security
- Where the SaaS product will handle RESTRICTED or higher data, contractually require that vendor personnel with administrative or data access hold appropriate clearances/vetting, or that compensating controls (e.g. logging, NZ-based support only) are in place.

## 3. Ongoing Assurance (Post-Contract)

- Incorporate the SaaS product into your agency's security risk register and System Security Plan / Security Risk Management Plan documentation.
- Schedule periodic reassessment of the vendor (e.g. annually, or upon renewal), including re-checking certifications and any reported incidents.
- Monitor for changes in the vendor's sub-processor list, ownership, or hosting location that might affect your risk position.
- Ensure the vendor is included in your agency's incident response and business continuity testing/exercises where the service is critical.

## Summary Checklist

- [ ] Data classification identified and risk-assessed
- [ ] Vendor certifications and security evidence reviewed (ISO 27001, SOC 2, etc.)
- [ ] Data location/sovereignty confirmed and offshore risk assessed if applicable
- [ ] Shared responsibility model understood and agency-side controls planned
- [ ] Contract includes encryption, access control, and audit rights clauses
- [ ] Contract includes mandatory incident notification with defined timeframes
- [ ] Contract includes data return/destruction and exit/portability provisions
- [ ] Sub-processor flow-down and change-notification clauses included
- [ ] Personnel security requirements included if handling RESTRICTED+ data
- [ ] Ongoing vendor reassessment scheduled post go-live

## Bottom Line

Your agency retains accountability for the security of its data even when using a SaaS product, so due diligence should assess the vendor's certifications, data location, and shared-responsibility posture before procurement, and the contract should lock in encryption, access control, breach notification, audit rights, sub-processor transparency, and clean exit/data-return provisions. The rigour of these requirements should scale with the classification of the data involved — treat any RESTRICTED-level use with the same seriousness as an offshore hosting or C&A decision.

*This is general guidance based on NZISM outsourcing/cloud principles. Confirm current NZISM control references and any All-of-Government procurement panel requirements with your agency's CISO/ITSM and procurement team before finalising vendor contracts.*
Prompt: What penalties do we actually face for personal data violations in Vietnam as of late 2026?
With Skill
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 5/5 assertions passed (100%)
