The Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) entered into force on 10 December 2024 but rolls out on a staggered timeline, and September 2026 happens to sit right at one of the key inflection points. Here's the picture, split into what's live now versus what's still ahead.

Already in force / applies now (as of September 2026):

1. Reporting obligations (Article 14) — applicable since 11 September 2026 (21 months after entry into force). This is the big one that just kicked in and is likely the reason for your question. Manufacturers of products with digital elements sold in the EU must now notify ENISA (which relays to your national CSIRT and market surveillance authorities) of:
   - Actively exploited vulnerabilities: 24-hour early warning, 72-hour follow-up notification, 14-day final report after a fix is available.
   - Severe incidents affecting the product's security: same 24h/72h structure, with a final report within one month.
   You also have a parallel duty to inform affected users without undue delay. This obligation is live today and is not waiting for 2027 — if you have a qualifying vulnerability or incident right now, the clock is running.

2. Conformity assessment body designation (Article 43-ish machinery) — applicable since 11 June 2026 (18 months after entry into force). Member states can now designate/notify conformity assessment bodies ("notified bodies") under the CRA, so the infrastructure for third-party assessment is starting to come online. This matters if your product needs mandatory third-party assessment (Class II important products, or Class I products without full harmonized-standard coverage) — you can begin engaging notified bodies now, and probably should, given expected capacity constraints closer to 2027.

3. General good-practice expectations. Even though the substantive essential requirements (Annex I) and CE-marking machinery aren't legally mandatory until December 2027, market expectations, procurement requirements, and your own risk exposure mean you should already be building: vulnerability-handling processes, SBOM practices, secure-by-design documentation, and incident-response playbooks — because (a) the reporting obligations above only work if you already have the internal muscle to detect and assess incidents/vulnerabilities quickly, and (b) you won't be able to stand up compliant Annex I documentation and processes overnight in late 2027.

Still ahead:

4. Full application — 11 December 2027 (36 months after entry into force). This is when the bulk of the CRA becomes binding: the Annex I essential requirements (secure by design/default, vulnerability handling, secure update mechanisms, etc.), the conformity assessment obligations proper (self-assessment or notified-body routes depending on classification), CE marking, EU Declarations of Conformity, technical documentation requirements, and the due-diligence obligations on importers and distributors (checking manufacturers have done their conformity assessment, CE marking is affixed, documentation exists, etc.). After this date, products with digital elements generally cannot be placed on the EU market without CRA conformity.

5. Transitional treatment of products already on the market. Products with digital elements already placed on the market before 11 December 2027 are generally not required to retroactively meet the full CRA regime unless they undergo a "substantial modification" after that date — but the Article 14 reporting obligations apply regardless of when the product was placed on the market, since reporting obligations are tied to the manufacturer's ongoing awareness of vulnerabilities/incidents, not to a product's original compliance date. That's an important nuance: even a pre-2024 product still being sold or supported today is inside the reporting regime now.

Bottom line for "right now" (September 2026): your live, binding obligation is the Article 14 vulnerability/incident reporting regime — get your CSIRT/ENISA reporting channel, 24/72-hour internal escalation process, and user-notification templates operational immediately if they aren't already. Your December 2027 obligation is the full essential-requirements/CE-marking/conformity-assessment package — treat the next 15 months as your build-out runway, including notified-body engagement if your product needs third-party assessment. I'd recommend confirming your product's Annex III classification (default / Class I / Class II) soon, since that determines how much of the 2027 workload is self-manageable versus dependent on third-party assessment capacity that is likely to tighten as the deadline approaches.

The CRA reporting platform — the ENISA Single Reporting Platform (SRP), at portal.cra-srp.enisa.europa.eu — has been live since 11 September 2026, so this is now an operational onboarding task, not a future-planning item. Here's the walkthrough.

**Who registers:**
Your organisation designates an **Assigned Representative (AR)** to handle CRA reporting. This isn't necessarily your CISO or a specific named role by regulation — it's whoever your organisation assigns to hold this responsibility, typically someone in security/compliance with authority to file regulatory notifications on the company's behalf. The first person to register becomes the **Primary AR**; your organisation can subsequently add up to **20 Secondary ARs**, which is useful if you want regional teams, an on-call rotation, or backup coverage so reporting isn't blocked by one person's availability during a 24-hour incident window.

If you're a **non-EU manufacturer**, the registration responsibility cascades: your EU **authorised representative** registers first; if you don't have one, it falls to your **importer**, then your **distributor**, then — as a last resort — **most affected users**. Confirm now which entity in your supply chain is positioned to register, rather than discovering the gap during an actual incident.

**How registration works:**
1. The AR creates an **EU Login account** (the EU's shared authentication system) — **multi-factor authentication is required**, so make sure whoever you designate has MFA set up and isn't going to be locked out at 2am during an incident.
2. During registration, the AR selects the **CSIRT Designated as Coordinator (CDaC)** — this is the national CSIRT of your **Member State of main establishment** (Article 14(7)). If you operate across multiple member states, "main establishment" needs a clear internal answer before you register, not during your first filing.
3. The AR accepts the platform's **legal agreement** to complete registration and becomes the Primary AR, with the option to add Secondary ARs afterward.
4. **CSIRT validation runs in parallel**, not as a gate — the SRP allows up to **20 notifications to be filed before verification completes**. This matters practically: don't assume you need to wait for account approval before you can file an urgent 24-hour early warning. Register and file; validation catches up in the background.

**ENISA's own guidance on timing:** register **when a notification is actually needed**, not pre-emptively for its own sake. That said, "when needed" during a live incident is the worst time to be figuring out EU Login/MFA setup and deciding who your main establishment's CSIRT is — so the practical reading is: do the organisational groundwork now (decide who your AR(s) will be, confirm your main establishment and its CSIRT, get EU Login/MFA provisioned) so that the actual SRP registration click-through, when you need it, takes minutes rather than becoming its own bottleneck inside a 24-hour clock.

**What happens once you're filing:**
Notifications route simultaneously to your CDaC and to ENISA (unless Particular Exceptional Circumstances apply under Article 16(2), with dissemination-delay rules set out in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/881). This means one filing satisfies both your national CSIRT and the EU-level coordinator — you don't file twice.

**If the platform is down when you need to report:**
Contact your **designated CSIRT directly** to meet your deadline — the 24-hour and 72-hour clocks don't pause for platform outages. Once the SRP is restored, you must still **file the notification through the SRP** to formally close it out; the direct CSIRT contact is a stopgap for the deadline, not a substitute for the record in the platform.

**Current platform limitations to plan around:**
- **English-only interface** — if your compliance/incident response team's working language isn't English, build in a translation step now rather than during a live filing.
- **No API** — this is a manual, browser-based workflow today. If your incident response tooling assumes automated regulatory filing, you need a documented manual handoff step in your runbook instead.

**Companion resources:** the European Commission's Communication C(2026) 5252 (27 July 2026) and the Commission's CRA FAQs provide additional operational guidance on the SRP and reporting expectations — worth reviewing alongside your onboarding.

**Practical checklist to onboard now:**
1. Decide Primary AR + any Secondary ARs (up to 20) and confirm they have EU Login + MFA ready.
2. Confirm your Member State of main establishment and its designated CSIRT (or, if non-EU, confirm which entity in your chain — authorised rep → importer → distributor → users — registers).
3. Register on the SRP now that you have an active need (per ENISA's guidance), rather than waiting until mid-incident.
4. Document a fallback procedure: direct CSIRT contact details, kept current, for platform-outage scenarios.
5. Build the manual filing step into your incident response runbook given the no-API/English-only constraints.

This is general compliance guidance, not legal advice — confirm your main-establishment determination and AR designation with counsel if your organisation's EU corporate structure is at all ambiguous.

Onboarding to CRA reporting isn't a single self-service "create an account" flow the way, say, a SaaS vendor portal is — it's built around ENISA's single reporting platform (mandated by Article 16 of the CRA) that channels notifications to national CSIRTs and market surveillance authorities. Since this infrastructure is still relatively new (the underlying reporting obligation only became applicable on 11 September 2026), expect some friction and jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction variation as it matures. Here's how to approach it.

Who registers. The obligation to report sits with the manufacturer of the product with digital elements (Article 14). If you're a non-EU manufacturer, your EU-based authorized representative can also be a point of contact, and importers/distributors have secondary obligations to inform manufacturers/authorities if they become aware of a vulnerability or incident, but the primary registrant and reporter is the manufacturer. In practice, the entity or role that should register is whoever owns your product security / PSIRT function — the team responsible for vulnerability handling and incident response — since they'll be the ones filing under time pressure.

How to register/onboard, practically:
1. Identify your "home" CSIRT. Under both NIS2 and the CRA, each manufacturer typically routes through the CSIRT designated as coordinator in the member state where it is established (or, for non-EU manufacturers, the state of their authorized representative). Start by contacting that national CSIRT/single point of contact directly — most member states have a national cybersecurity agency (e.g., a national CERT/CSIRT) with published guidance and intake channels, and many are actively onboarding manufacturers ahead of/around the CRA reporting obligation coming into force.
2. Register with ENISA's reporting platform once access is available to you. ENISA is responsible for building and operating the single reporting platform under Article 16, intended to let manufacturers submit early warnings, notifications, and final reports in a structured way and have that information automatically routed to the relevant CSIRT and market surveillance authority. Because this is a relatively new piece of shared EU infrastructure, availability, exact registration steps (e.g., whether it requires an EU Login/eIDAS-based identity, a company registration process, API access for high-volume reporters, etc.) may still be rolling out unevenly — check ENISA's official CRA guidance pages and your national CSIRT for the current registration procedure rather than assuming a single universal portal experience already exists everywhere.
3. Prepare your internal reporting workflow before you need it. Regardless of platform mechanics, you need: a defined "become aware" trigger, an on-call/escalation path that can produce a 24-hour early warning, a template covering the minimum required fields (nature of vulnerability/incident, affected product(s)/versions, member states affected, exploitation status), and a document trail. Registering your team's contact details and authentication credentials with the CSIRT/platform ahead of an actual incident avoids losing time during the critical first 24 hours.

What if the platform is down when you need it. The CRA's reporting deadlines are not suspended just because ENISA's platform has an outage — the obligation is to notify "without undue delay" and within the stated hour/day windows, so you need a fallback:
- Contact your national CSIRT directly through its published out-of-platform channel (phone, dedicated incident email, or an alternate web form) — national CSIRTs generally maintain 24/7 contact points for exactly this kind of situation, independent of the EU-level platform.
- Document the outage and your attempted submission time/timestamp — this evidence will matter if a market surveillance authority later questions timeliness; regulators generally expect good-faith efforts and reasonable alternative channels to be used, not silence, when the primary system is unavailable.
- Submit the full notification through the platform as soon as it's restored, referencing your earlier direct CSIRT contact so the record is complete and continuous.
- If you have a NIS2 relationship with the same CSIRT (many manufacturers of important products also have obligations or informal relationships under NIS2), you may already have an established direct channel you can use as your default fallback — worth confirming this mapping in advance rather than during an actual incident.

Because the operational and platform-level details here are still being finalized/rolled out at the EU and member-state level, I'd treat this as a live-document problem: assign someone to monitor ENISA's and your national CSIRT's published guidance specifically for CRA reporting-platform mechanics over the next several months, since exact registration steps and outage-fallback procedures are likely to be clarified and possibly changed as the system matures toward the December 2027 full-application deadline.

# Saudi Market Entry — Applicability & First 90 Days

A couple of quick confirmations that would sharpen this (I've made reasonable working assumptions where you haven't told me, flagged below — correct me if any are wrong):

- I'm assuming you are **not** SAMA-, CST-, or CMA-licensed (i.e., you're not becoming a payment institution yourselves — you'll use a licensed Saudi/regional payment gateway) and you are **not** designated Critical National Infrastructure (CNI).
- I'm assuming your Saudi online store will process ordinary customer data (name, contact, address, order/payment metadata) — not health, biometric, or other "sensitive" categories under Saudi law.
- I'm assuming you'll host on a mainstream cloud provider (in- or out-of-Kingdom) rather than operating your own cloud infrastructure.

## Applicability Matrix

| Instrument | Regulator | Applies to you? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Saudi PDPL** (Royal Decree M/19, as amended by M/148) | SDAIA | **Yes — mandatory** | You will process personal data of Saudi residents (customers) through your new entity and online store. PDPL applies regardless of where the processing entity sits, and is fully enforced since 14 September 2024. |
| **NCA ECC-2:2024** (Essential Cybersecurity Controls) | NCA | **No — recommended only** | Mandatory only for government entities/subsidiaries and CNI operators. As a private e-commerce retailer with no government contracts, ECC is best-practice, not a legal obligation — but it's the standard NCA/customers/partners will benchmark you against informally. |
| **NCA CCC** (Cloud Cybersecurity Controls) | NCA | **No** | Only binds CSPs serving, or cloud tenants that are, ECC-covered entities. You are neither. |
| **CST Cloud Computing Regulatory Framework** | CST | **No** (as a cloud tenant) | This binds cloud service *providers* operating in KSA and sets residency rules for Level 3–4 customer data. You're a tenant buying cloud services, not a CSP, so it doesn't bind you directly — but it governs *your provider's* obligations and shapes where they can legally host Saudi customer data if you go with a locally registered CSP. |
| **SAMA Cyber Security Framework** | SAMA | **No** | Applies to SAMA-licensed banks/insurers/financing companies/fintechs. You're not becoming a payment licensee. |
| **CMA Cybersecurity Guidelines** | CMA | **No** | Capital markets only. |

**Bottom line:** your binding Saudi compliance obligation is the **PDPL**, administered by **SDAIA**. Everything else (ECC, NCA reporting) is voluntary hygiene that's still worth doing because it signals maturity to Saudi partners, insurers, and increasingly to enterprise/government customers you may pursue later.

Note: standing up a Saudi entity and e-commerce operation also triggers general commercial-law requirements (MISA foreign-investment licensing, Ministry of Commerce e-commerce registration/consumer-protection rules, Zakat/tax registration) that sit outside cybersecurity/data-protection GRC and outside what I can authoritatively detail here — loop in Saudi corporate counsel for those in parallel.

## First 90 Days

**Days 1–30 — PDPL foundations (SDAIA)**
- Register as a data controller on SDAIA's **National Data Governance Platform** (dgp.sdaia.gov.sa).
- Build a **Record of Processing Activities (RoPA)** covering the online store: what customer data you collect, purpose, retention, who it flows to (payment gateway, logistics, marketing tools, EU HQ systems).
- Determine your **lawful basis** per data flow — consent as the default; contract performance for order fulfillment; legitimate interest (added by M/148) is available for most marketing/analytics uses but **not for sensitive data**.
- Draft/localize your **privacy notice** (Arabic + English) — purpose limitation and minimization built in from day one.
- Assess whether SDAIA rules require a **DPO appointment** given the scale of your processing (retail at volume typically triggers this).
- Stand up a **breach response procedure** with a hard **72-hour SDAIA notification clock**, plus a threshold test for when affected customers must also be notified (risk-based).

**Days 30–60 — Cross-border data flows and vendor contracts**
- Since you're a European retailer, customer data will likely flow back to EU-based systems (ERP, CRM, analytics, group reporting). Establish a lawful **transfer mechanism**: SDAIA-assessed adequacy (unlikely to cover EU→other-EU internal flows the way you'd want; check current SDAIA adequacy list), **SDAIA Standard Contractual Clauses** (C2C/C2P/P2C/P2P modules as appropriate), or **Binding Common Rules** if this is an intra-group transfer program.
- Paper your vendor relationships (payment gateway, cloud host, logistics, marketing/CDP tools) with **DPAs** reflecting PDPL processor obligations, not just GDPR ones — the two overlap heavily but aren't identical (SDAIA registration, Arabic artifacts, and the 72-hour clock are Saudi-specific).
- Confirm your cloud provider's hosting location and residency posture. You have no legal residency mandate (you're not government/CNI, and customer data levels 3–4 residency rules bind your *CSP*, not you) — but many Saudi consumers and regulators view in-Kingdom or regional hosting favorably, so factor this into vendor selection even though it's not compulsory.

**Days 60–90 — Security baseline and cross-mapping**
- Adopt **NCA ECC-2:2024** as a voluntary best-practice baseline — you don't need full formal compliance, but pull the core hygiene: asset management, access control, encryption of data at rest/in transit, logging/monitoring, incident response, patch management, backup.
- **Cross-map your existing EU compliance work** (GDPR program, ISO 27001 if certified) to PDPL — most controllers find 70–80% evidence reuse is possible (privacy notices, RoPA, DSR handling, breach procedures), with the deltas being SDAIA-specific: platform registration, Arabic-language artifacts, the SDAIA transfer-mechanism paperwork, and the 72-hour notification channel (distinct from GDPR's 72-hour-to-supervisory-authority, but not automatically satisfied by your existing GDPR process).
- Run a light internal audit against your RoPA and privacy notice before go-live, and confirm your customer-facing consent flows (cookie/marketing consent) meet PDPL's consent standard, not just GDPR's.

## Enforcement context to plan around
PDPL enforcement is active and material: fines up to **SAR 5,000,000 per violation** (doubling for repeat violations), and criminal exposure up to **2 years' imprisonment** for unlawful disclosure of sensitive data. SDAIA's enforcement committees issued roughly 48 violation decisions in the first wave (2025–26), so this isn't a dormant law — budget real compliance effort, not a checkbox privacy notice.

**Dated item:** SDAIA ran a public consultation in April 2025 on proposed PDPL amendments (including graduated penalties). As of today (23 August 2026), those amendments are **not enacted** — build your compliance program on the current law and confirm directly with SDAIA before relying on any proposed changes.

# Saudi Arabia Compliance Roadmap for a European E-Commerce Retailer

*Disclaimer: This is general guidance based on publicly known regulatory frameworks, not legal advice. Engage Saudi outside counsel and a licensed Mudad/GOSI-registered advisor before launch.*

## 1. Regulatory Landscape That Applies to You

Even without government contracts, a foreign e-commerce retailer selling to Saudi consumers touches a wide set of regimes:

- **Foreign investment licensing** – Ministry of Investment (MISA, formerly SAGIA) license is required to legally establish and own a Saudi entity as a foreign investor.
- **Companies Law (2022)** – governs your legal form (typically an LLC), governance, capital, and reporting.
- **Commercial Registration (CR)** – Ministry of Commerce (MoC) registration, plus a National Address and Wasel registration.
- **E-Commerce Law (2019) and its Executive Regulations** – MoC rules on mandatory website disclosures (CR number, legal name, address, prices in SAR, contact details), return/refund policy, order confirmation, and marketing/advertising conduct.
- **Consumer Protection Law** – governs product quality, warranty, misleading advertising, and complaint handling; enforced by MoC.
- **Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL)** and its Implementing Regulations (SDAIA is the regulator) – applies to any processing of personal data of individuals in the Kingdom, including customer names, addresses, phone numbers, payment metadata, and order history. Enforcement is active as of late 2024, so you are already in scope.
- **SASO / SABER** – if you sell physical goods (electronics, toys, cosmetics, textiles, etc.), Saudi Standards, Metrology and Quality Organization (SASO) product conformity certificates must be issued through the SABER platform before goods clear customs.
- **ZATCA (Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority)** – VAT registration (15%) and mandatory e-invoicing (Fatoora), including phase 2 integration once you exceed the applicable revenue threshold. Customs duties apply to imported goods.
- **Payments** – SAMA regulates payment services; you will almost certainly integrate with a SAMA-licensed Payment Service Provider (PSP)/acquirer (e.g., a licensed gateway) rather than becoming a licensed PSP yourself, but your checkout flow, refund handling, and any stored card data must meet PCI DSS and SAMA's outsourcing expectations for your PSP relationship.
- **Anti-Commercial Fraud Law** – prohibits misleading claims about origin, quality, and pricing.
- **Anti-Cyber Crime Law** – relevant to how you secure customer data and respond to breaches.
- **Labor Law, Saudization (Nitaqat), and GOSI** – once you hire local staff, you must meet Saudization quotas for your company size/sector and register employees with GOSI for social insurance.
- **Municipal/business licensing** – warehouse, fulfillment center, or office locations need municipal (baladiya) licenses.

## 2. First 90 Days – Suggested Sequence

**Days 1–30: Legal and Regulatory Foundation**
- Finalize MISA investment license and MoC Commercial Registration.
- Register with ZATCA for VAT and confirm e-invoicing (Fatoora) system requirements for your billing software.
- Appoint (or contract) a Data Protection Officer / PDPL compliance owner and run an initial PDPL gap assessment covering: lawful basis for processing, data inventory, cross-border transfer exposure (especially if customer data flows back to EU servers), consent flows, and a breach-notification procedure (SDAIA notification obligations, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of a qualifying incident).
- Map current EU privacy notices/GDPR program against PDPL requirements – GDPR gives you a head start, but PDPL has distinct definitions of sensitive data, different consent standards, and its own data-subject-rights procedures.

**Days 31–60: Commercial and Product Readiness**
- Rebuild or localize the website: Arabic-language version, SAR pricing, mandatory MoC e-commerce disclosures, return/refund policy compliant with the E-Commerce Law, and clear terms of service.
- Begin SASO/SABER product certification for any physical SKUs; build this into your supply chain lead times since it can take several weeks per product category.
- Finalize your PSP/payment gateway integration and confirm it is SAMA-licensed; document the data flow and any PCI DSS obligations.
- Draft a PDPL-compliant privacy policy and cookie/consent banner; update your Data Processing Agreements with any vendors (fulfillment, marketing, analytics, cloud hosting) to reflect PDPL processor obligations.
- Assess data residency: decide whether customer data will be hosted in-Kingdom, in the EU, or in a hybrid model, and document the legal basis for any cross-border transfer under PDPL's transfer rules.

**Days 61–90: Operational Launch Readiness**
- Complete GOSI registration and Saudization planning for any local hires; confirm your Nitaqat category obligations.
- Finalize warehouse/fulfillment municipal licensing if you operate local logistics.
- Run an internal compliance dry-run: test the checkout flow for MoC disclosure compliance, test a simulated data subject access request, test your incident response plan against PDPL notification timelines.
- Put a recurring compliance calendar in place (VAT filings, PDPL record-of-processing updates, SASO certificate renewals, Nitaqat reporting) and assign internal owners.
- Consider engaging local counsel for a final pre-launch legal review of your Arabic terms and privacy policy, since MoC and SDAIA both scrutinize consumer-facing language.

## 3. Key Risk Areas to Watch
- PDPL enforcement is active and fines can be significant; treat this as equal priority to VAT/commercial registration, not an afterthought.
- SASO/SABER certification lead times are a common launch bottleneck for retailers — start early.
- Saudization quotas can affect your ability to hire expatriate staff quickly; plan headcount accordingly.

# SAMA-Licensed Fintech: Does NCA ECC Also Apply?

Short answer: **both frameworks can apply, and they stack rather than one displacing the other.** The SAMA Cyber Security Framework is mandatory for you regardless. Whether NCA ECC-2:2024 is *also* mandatory turns on one fact I don't have: **has NCA designated your systems as Critical National Infrastructure (CNI)?** I'll answer both branches below, plus the maturity-level question, which is unambiguous.

## Applicability Matrix

| Instrument | Regulator | Applies to you? |
|---|---|---|
| **SAMA Cyber Security Framework (CSF)** v1.0 | SAMA | **Yes — mandatory.** Binds all SAMA-regulated entities: banks, insurers, financing companies, credit bureaus, and licensed fintechs. No exceptions for license type. |
| **NCA ECC-2:2024** | NCA | **Conditional.** Mandatory only if NCA has designated you (or the systems/services you operate) as Critical National Infrastructure. Most licensed fintechs are not CNI-designated unless they operate systemically important payment infrastructure or rails. If not CNI, ECC is *recommended best practice*, not a legal mandate, for you. |
| **NCA CCC** (Cloud Cybersecurity Controls) | NCA | **Conditional, follows ECC.** If you're ECC-covered (CNI) and you use cloud infrastructure, CCC tenant-side controls apply. If not ECC-covered, CCC doesn't bind you, though your cloud provider may still be bound on the CSP side if they serve other ECC-covered clients. |
| **Saudi PDPL** | SDAIA | **Yes — mandatory.** You process Saudi residents' personal (and likely financial, which is not automatically "sensitive" under PDPL's specific categories but is treated carefully in practice) data as a fintech. Fully enforced since 14 September 2024, independent of your SAMA license. |
| **CST / CMA** | CST / CMA | **No**, unless you separately hold a CST cloud/telecom registration or a CMA capital-markets license. |

**Stacking rule:** if you *are* CNI-designated, you must satisfy SAMA CSF **and** NCA ECC-2:2024 simultaneously — these are cumulative regimes, not alternatives. There's no published deconfliction protocol between SAMA and NCA where their requirements overlap or appear to conflict; the practical approach is to maintain one internal control set mapped to both frameworks, satisfy whichever requirement is stricter on any given point, document the mapping, and engage both regulators directly if a genuine conflict arises rather than assuming either one's requirement supersedes the other's.

**If you're not sure of your CNI status:** confirm with SAMA/NCA directly — this determines whether ECC compliance reporting is a legal obligation or a voluntary maturity uplift for you. In the meantime, treat ECC as your target-state baseline regardless, since SAMA CSF and ECC overlap substantially in the controls they expect (governance, access control, incident management, third-party/cloud security).

## Maturity Level Required

This part is unambiguous under SAMA CSF:

- SAMA CSF uses a **six-level maturity model (0–5)**: 0 Non-existent → 1 Ad-hoc → 2 Repeatable but informal → **3 Structured & formalized** → 4 Managed & measurable → 5 Adaptive.
- **SAMA's minimum expectation is Level 3 — "Structured & formalized"**: defined, approved, and consistently implemented processes, not just informal or ad-hoc practices. This is the floor for compliance, assessed via periodic self-assessment plus SAMA reviews.
- In practice, entities handling higher transaction volumes, holding e-money/payment licenses, or otherwise carrying systemic importance often push toward **Level 4 (Managed & measurable)** — SAMA doesn't mandate this uniformly, but supervisory expectations tend to rise with risk profile, so don't treat Level 3 as a ceiling if your risk footprint is significant.
- If you are also ECC-covered (CNI), NCA ECC doesn't use the same 0–5 maturity scale — it's assessed as implemented / partially implemented / not implemented / not applicable per control, via NCA's compliance tool and self-assessment plus NCA audits. You'd need to satisfy both the SAMA maturity-3 floor and full ECC control implementation concurrently.

## SAMA CSF structure, for context
Four domains: (1) Cyber Security Leadership & Governance, (2) Cyber Security Risk Management & Compliance, (3) Cyber Security Operations & Technology, (4) Third-Party Cyber Security. Adjacent SAMA instruments you're also likely subject to as a licensee: the **IT Governance Framework**, the **Business Continuity Management Framework**, and **Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles (2022)** — these ride alongside CSF rather than replacing it.

## Recommended next step
1. Confirm CNI designation status directly with NCA/SAMA — this is the single fact that changes your legal obligation set.
2. Regardless of the answer, benchmark your current controls against SAMA CSF Level 3 requirements now, since that's mandatory either way.
3. If CNI-designated, start an ECC-2:2024 gap assessment in parallel (domain/subdomain based — I can build that gap table if you share current-state detail).

# NCA ECC vs. SAMA Cybersecurity Framework for a SAMA-Licensed Fintech

*Disclaimer: General guidance based on publicly known regulatory structures, not legal or regulatory advice. Confirm your exact scope directly with SAMA and, where relevant, the National Cybersecurity Authority (NCA).*

## Short Answer

As a SAMA-licensed fintech, your **primary and mandatory cybersecurity framework is the SAMA Cybersecurity Framework (SAMA CSF)**, not a direct standalone obligation to the NCA Essential Cybersecurity Controls (ECC). SAMA is your sector regulator and the NCA has historically deferred day-to-day supervision of financial-sector entities to SAMA, since SAMA CSF was built to be broadly consistent with (and in many places more prescriptive than) the NCA's national baseline controls. That said, the NCA ECC still matters to you in three ways:

1. **SAMA CSF was designed with strong alignment to NCA ECC and international standards (NIST CSF, ISO 27001, PCI DSS)** — most ECC control objectives are already embedded in SAMA CSF, so compliance work overlaps heavily rather than being duplicative.
2. **If any part of your operations is classified as Critical National Infrastructure (CNI)** — for example, if you operate payment-switching or settlement infrastructure deemed systemically important — the NCA can assert direct oversight or require ECC compliance in coordination with SAMA.
3. **NCA periodically updates the national baseline (e.g., ECC-2:2024)**, and SAMA typically updates SAMA CSF to stay harmonized; you should track both publications and re-run your control mapping whenever either is revised, since gaps can open up between updates.

**Practical guidance:** treat SAMA CSF as your governing framework and audit target, but maintain a control-mapping matrix between SAMA CSF and the current NCA ECC version so you can demonstrate coverage of both if either SAMA or NCA asks, and so you catch any ECC-specific control that SAMA CSF hasn't yet absorbed.

## Maturity Level Expected

SAMA CSF uses a maturity model (similar in structure to COBIT/CMM-style scales, roughly: 0 – Non-Existent, 1 – Ad-hoc, 2 – Repeatable but Informal, 3 – Structured/Defined, 4 – Managed and Measurable, 5 – Adaptive/Optimized).

- **Baseline expectation for regulated financial institutions, including licensed fintechs:** Maturity Level 3 ("Defined/Structured") across the SAMA CSF domains at minimum. This means controls are formally documented, approved, communicated, and consistently applied — not just performed ad hoc.
- **Higher expectation for systemically important or higher-risk institutions** (larger banks, payment infrastructure providers, or fintechs handling large transaction volumes/customer funds at scale): SAMA generally expects progression toward **Level 4 ("Managed and Measurable")**, where controls are actively monitored with metrics, and effectiveness is regularly reviewed by management.
- **New/smaller licensed fintechs** are typically expected to reach Level 3 within a defined ramp-up period after licensing (SAMA usually sets an implementation timeline in the license conditions or supervisory letters), with an expectation of continuous improvement toward Level 4 over subsequent assessment cycles.

Your actual target should be confirmed against your specific license type and any maturity target communicated in your SAMA license conditions or supervisory correspondence, since SAMA can set entity-specific expectations that differ from the general baseline (e.g., higher targets for institutions handling larger transaction volumes or holding customer funds directly).

## Recommended Next Steps
1. Obtain the current SAMA CSF version and confirm your assigned maturity target with your SAMA relationship/supervisory contact.
2. Build (or update) a control-mapping matrix: SAMA CSF domains ↔ current NCA ECC version ↔ ISO 27001/NIST CSF if you hold or reference those certifications.
3. Run a formal self-assessment against SAMA CSF maturity levels per domain (not just a binary compliant/non-compliant check), and prioritize remediation for any domain scoring below your target level.
4. Establish a recurring review cadence (at least annual, ideally aligned with SAMA's supervisory review cycle) to re-baseline against updates to both SAMA CSF and NCA ECC.
5. If you operate or plan to operate payment infrastructure that could be deemed critical infrastructure, proactively confirm with SAMA/NCA whether direct ECC obligations attach to that specific system.

# Global SaaS Hosting a Saudi Government Ministry — Compliance & Residency

A few facts would sharpen the specifics, and I've made working assumptions where you haven't told me — flag anything that's wrong:

- I'm assuming your company does **not** currently hold a CST cloud registration or KSA-based infrastructure (you're a "global SaaS provider" planning to enter, not already licensed).
- I'm assuming the ministry workload will include the ministry's operational/citizen data, which likely includes Saudi residents' personal data.
- I'm assuming the **data classification** hasn't been formally set yet with the ministry — this is the single fact that will most determine your obligations, so get it nailed down early (see below).

## Applicability Matrix

| Instrument | Regulator | Applies to you? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CST Cloud Computing Regulatory Framework v3** | CST | **Yes — mandatory** | You are acting as a Cloud Service Provider (CSP) hosting workloads in/for KSA. CSP registration with CST is required to legally operate. Your registration class (Qualification / A / B / C) determines which customer data levels you're permitted to host. |
| **NCA CCC** (Cloud Cybersecurity Controls) | NCA | **Yes — mandatory (CSP-side controls)** | You're serving an entity (a government ministry) that is itself mandatorily ECC-covered. CCC binds CSPs serving ECC-covered tenants — you'll need to implement the CSP-role controls (role marker "P" in control IDs), while the ministry carries the tenant-side ("T") controls and remains accountable for its own data. |
| **NCA ECC-2:2024** | NCA | **Indirectly — the ministry's obligation, but it constrains you** | ECC is mandatory for the government ministry itself. It doesn't bind you directly as an external CSP, but the ministry will require contractual evidence that your service supports its ECC compliance (this is standard practice for NCA-regulated cloud engagements with government). |
| **Saudi PDPL** | SDAIA | **Yes — mandatory** | If the workload processes any personal data of Saudi residents (near-certain for a ministry system), PDPL applies to you as the processor (and possibly joint controller depending on contract terms), independent of your CST/CCC obligations. Fully enforced since 14 September 2024. |
| **NCA DCC-1:2022** (Data Cybersecurity Controls) | NCA | **Likely relevant** | Data-lifecycle protections (classification, handling, storage, disposal) for ECC-covered entities and their service providers — routes alongside CCC for this engagement. |
| **SAMA / CMA** | SAMA / CMA | **No** | Not applicable unless the ministry is itself a financial or capital-markets regulator (not stated). |

**Stacking rule:** you face CST registration + CCC (CSP-side) + PDPL (processor obligations) + likely DCC, concurrently — not a choice between them. Treat this as one combined compliance program for the engagement, not four separate initiatives.

## Where must the data live?

This is governed by two overlapping rules, and for a government ministry the answer is strict:

1. **Government data localization is exclusive under the CST framework**: government workloads must remain **in-Kingdom (Saudi Arabia)**, with only narrow, specifically-approved exceptions. As a practical matter, plan for **100% in-Kingdom hosting** of this workload — don't architect around exceptions unless the ministry and CST explicitly grant one in writing.
2. **Cloud levels are tied to data classification** (Top Secret / Secret / Confidential / Public) under both NCA CCC and the CST framework. Higher classification (Secret/Top Secret) requires higher-assurance cloud environments and stricter controls; even at the lower end, **CST customer data Levels 3–4 require in-Kingdom residency** regardless of classification label. Given this is a government ministry, assume at minimum "Confidential" classification driving Level 3+ requirements unless the ministry tells you otherwise in writing.

**Action item:** get the ministry to formally classify the workload's data (Top Secret/Secret/Confidential/Public and the corresponding CST data level) before you finalize architecture — this single input determines your required cloud level, your CST registration class, and your residency design. Don't proceed on an assumed classification.

## What you need to do, sequenced

1. **CST registration** — apply for CSP registration at the class that covers the data levels the ministry needs (likely Class A/B given government data, pending classification confirmation). This typically requires establishing in-Kingdom infrastructure/presence — a "global" footprint without a KSA region won't satisfy this.
2. **NCA CCC CSP-side controls** — implement and evidence the provider-side control set; be ready to support the ministry's own ECC compliance reporting with technical evidence, attestations, and audit cooperation.
3. **PDPL processor posture** — execute a PDPL-compliant data processing agreement with the ministry, confirm lawful basis and purpose limitation on your side, and build breach-notification cooperation into the contract (SDAIA's 72-hour clock runs from when the controller/processor becomes aware — your incident response needs to feed the ministry fast enough for them to meet it, or you may have direct notification duties depending on contract terms).
4. **Data lifecycle controls (DCC)** — classification-driven handling, storage, and disposal procedures aligned to NCA's Data Cybersecurity Controls.
5. **Contractual/architecture lock-in** — no cross-border replication, backup, or support-tooling data flows that would move ministry data outside the Kingdom, including logging, telemetry, and support-ticket attachments — these are common residency leaks in global SaaS architectures.

## Penalties/enforcement context
Beyond CST/NCA enforcement mechanics (not separately detailed here), PDPL violations carry fines up to **SAR 5,000,000 per violation** (doubling for repeats) and criminal exposure up to **2 years' imprisonment** for unlawful disclosure of sensitive data — relevant if ministry data includes sensitive categories (health, biometric, criminal/security, etc.).

**Dated item:** proposed PDPL amendments from SDAIA's April 2025 consultation are **not enacted as of today (23 August 2026)** — build on the current law and confirm status with SDAIA before relying on anticipated changes.

# Compliance Requirements for a Global SaaS Provider Hosting a Saudi Government Ministry

*Disclaimer: General guidance based on publicly known Saudi cloud and cybersecurity regulatory structures, not legal advice. Government hosting engagements typically require a formal compliance review with CST/NCA and the specific ministry's IT governance team before contracting.*

## 1. Framework Overview

Hosting workloads for a Saudi government ministry puts you squarely inside the Kingdom's most stringent regulatory tier. The key regimes are:

- **Cloud Computing Regulatory Framework (CCRF)**, issued by the Communications, Space & Technology Commission (CST, formerly CITC). This is the master framework governing cloud service providers (CSPs) and cloud service customers (CSCs) in Saudi Arabia, including data classification tiers and hosting location rules.
- **NCA Essential Cybersecurity Controls (ECC)** — the national cybersecurity baseline, mandatory for government entities and their contractors/service providers handling government data.
- **NCA Cloud Cybersecurity Controls (CCC)** — a cloud-specific control set issued by the National Cybersecurity Authority that applies specifically to CSPs and CSCs handling government or sensitive data in cloud environments; this sits on top of the general ECC baseline.
- **Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL)** and its Implementing Regulations (SDAIA) — applies because ministry systems will almost certainly process personal data of Saudi citizens/residents.
- **National Data Management Office (NDMO) / SDAIA data classification policy** — government data must be classified (e.g., public, restricted, confidential, top secret/highly sensitive) and handled according to the rules attached to that classification tier.
- **CST licensing requirements** — providing cloud/telecom infrastructure services in the Kingdom generally requires either a CST-issued license or delivery through a CST-licensed/accredited local partner.

## 2. Where the Data Must Live

The CCRF classifies government and government-related data into tiers, and the hosting-location rules scale with sensitivity:

- **Lower-sensitivity/public data**: may in some cases be hosted outside the Kingdom, but this is the exception, not the norm, for government ministry workloads.
- **Sensitive/restricted government data**: generally must be hosted **inside Saudi Arabia**, in a facility that meets CST/NCA accreditation requirements.
- **Highly sensitive/classified or national-security-relevant data**: must be hosted **in-Kingdom with no foreign remote access**, stricter personnel vetting, and often requires the CSP to operate through a wholly Saudi-incorporated entity or joint venture with in-country data center infrastructure.

**Practical implication:** for a government ministry engagement, assume from the outset that in-country hosting will be required unless the ministry's data classification review explicitly designates the workload as low-sensitivity/public. Global hyperscalers active in this space have generally addressed this by standing up dedicated in-Kingdom cloud regions (with local data center infrastructure and, in some cases, local partnership structures) specifically to meet government/sovereign hosting requirements — you will likely need an equivalent local presence or partnership rather than serving the ministry from an offshore region.

## 3. What You Must Comply With

1. **Data classification** — work with the ministry (or independently, per NDMO/SDAIA policy) to classify the workload's data before deciding architecture; this classification drives every downstream hosting and access-control decision.
2. **CST accreditation/licensing** — confirm whether you need to become a CST-licensed CSP directly, or whether you can operate through an existing CST-licensed/"Government Authorized" cloud provider as your underlying infrastructure. Many foreign SaaS vendors deliver into Saudi government customers by running on top of an accredited local cloud region rather than obtaining their own infrastructure license.
3. **NCA ECC baseline controls** — governance, asset management, identity and access management, cryptography, logging/monitoring, incident management, business continuity, and physical security controls all apply to the systems hosting ministry data.
4. **NCA Cloud Cybersecurity Controls (CCC)** — additional cloud-specific requirements covering shared responsibility definitions between CSP and CSC, tenant isolation, cloud-specific incident response, and data sanitization/destruction on contract termination.
5. **PDPL compliance** — lawful basis for processing, data subject rights handling, breach notification to SDAIA (generally within a short window, commonly cited as 72 hours for qualifying incidents), and strict controls on any cross-border transfer of personal data — cross-border transfer of government-related personal data is highly restricted and typically requires specific government/regulatory approval, if it is permitted at all.
6. **No unauthorized offshoring** — do not assume you can replicate, back up, or support the workload from outside the Kingdom without explicit contractual and regulatory approval; remote access by non-Kingdom personnel to production government data is often specifically restricted or prohibited depending on classification.
7. **Contractual/procurement requirements** — Saudi government procurement often layers additional requirements (e.g., local content/IKTVA-style requirements, escrow or exit provisions, audit rights for NCA/CST, and specific SLAs) on top of the regulatory baseline; review the ministry's RFP/contract terms closely as they may exceed the regulatory minimum.

## 4. Recommended Path Forward
1. Engage the ministry's IT/security team early to obtain (or jointly perform) the data classification for the specific workload — this single step determines your hosting architecture.
2. Determine whether to deliver via an existing CST-accredited/government-authorized local cloud provider (fastest path) versus pursuing your own CST license and in-Kingdom infrastructure build-out (longer, higher-investment path).
3. Perform a gap assessment against NCA ECC + NCA CCC using your current security program (ISO 27001, SOC 2, etc. are good starting points but do not substitute for these Saudi-specific frameworks).
4. Build a PDPL-compliant data processing and cross-border transfer position, in writing, before contract signature — this is frequently the item that stalls government cloud deals late in procurement.
5. Confirm personnel/access requirements (e.g., whether only Saudi-based or Saudi-vetted personnel may have production access) before committing to a support model.

# Unauthorized Disclosure of 40,000 Customer Records — Your Obligations

This is a personal data breach under Saudi law, and the clock is already running. Before the detail, a few clarifying facts would sharpen the exact obligation set (I've proceeded on reasonable assumptions, flagged below):

- I'm assuming your company is a **private commercial entity**, not SAMA/CST/CMA-licensed and not a government subsidiary or CNI operator — tell me if that's wrong, since it would add SAMA or NCA incident-reporting duties on top of what's below.
- I'm assuming the 40,000 records belong to **Saudi residents** (if a meaningful share are foreign nationals outside KSA, PDPL still applies to the KSA-resident subset regardless of where your company sits).
- National ID numbers are direct identifiers with serious fraud/impersonation potential. Saudi PDPL's specific "sensitive data" category (health, genetic, biometric, location, criminal/security data, and data revealing racial/ethnic/religious/political information) doesn't explicitly list national ID as such — but confirm this classification with counsel, since it changes whether the criminal-exposure provisions below apply. Regardless of that classification question, this is unambiguously a **reportable personal data breach**.

## Applicable law
| Instrument | Regulator | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **Saudi PDPL** (Royal Decree M/19, as amended by M/148) | SDAIA | Governs this incident directly — unauthorized disclosure of personal data by your workforce to an unauthorized third party, breach notification duties, and penalty exposure. |
| **NCA / SAMA / CST reporting** | NCA/SAMA/CST | Only relevant if you're government-subsidiary/CNI (NCA), SAMA-licensed (SAMA), or a CSP (CST) — confirm your status, as this would add parallel incident-reporting obligations. |

## What happened, in PDPL terms
An employee disclosed personal data (including what functions as a highly sensitive identifier — national ID) to an external party **without authorization and without a lawful basis for that specific disclosure**. This is a breach regardless of intent — it's not something a data processing agreement or consent notice retroactively covers, because the disclosure fell outside your stated purposes and outside any lawful basis you had for sharing with that vendor. Treat this as a **confirmed personal data breach**, not merely a "possible" one.

## Immediate steps (hours, not days)

1. **Contain**: revoke the employee's ability to send further data externally where feasible, and secure the systems/exports involved. Do not wait for the investigation to finish before containing exposure.
2. **Engage the vendor immediately and in writing**: demand written confirmation that they will not use, further disclose, or retain the data, and request immediate deletion with certification. If a data processing agreement didn't exist before this transfer (likely, since it was "unauthorized"), you have no contractual leverage compelling their cooperation — this is a real limitation; involve legal counsel now to explore what recourse exists (breach of confidence, unlawful processing claims against the recipient under PDPL if they knowingly process improperly obtained data).
3. **Preserve evidence**: email logs, access logs, file/export logs, the employee's role and access rights at the time, and timeline of discovery. This underpins both your regulatory notification and any internal disciplinary/legal action against the employee.
4. **Scope the breach precisely**: confirm exactly 40,000 records, exactly which fields (national ID number plus what else — name, DOB, contact, financial data?), and whether the vendor has already used or redistributed it. The presence of national ID numbers at this scale should be treated as high risk to data subjects (identity theft, fraud, impersonation) regardless of the sensitive-data classification question above.

## Regulatory notification — the 72-hour clock
- **Notify SDAIA within 72 hours of becoming aware** of the breach, via SDAIA's **National Data Governance Platform**. This clock started when someone in your organization became aware of the unauthorized transfer — confirm that timestamp precisely, since "awareness" (not "root-cause-confirmed") is what starts it.
- **Notify affected data subjects** where the breach poses risk to them. At 40,000 records including national IDs, this crosses the risk threshold — plan for direct customer notification (or public notice if direct contact isn't feasible at that scale) describing what happened, what data was involved, and what protective steps customers should take (e.g., monitoring for identity misuse).
- If your company is separately NCA/SAMA/CST-regulated (see assumption above), those regulators likely have their own incident-reporting timelines and channels running in parallel to the SDAIA notification — don't assume one filing satisfies all regulators.

## Internal accountability
- This was caused by an employee action, but under PDPL your company as **controller** carries the compliance obligation regardless of individual fault — the employee's unauthorized act doesn't shift the notification duty or the exposure away from the company.
- Separately, pursue the employee matter through your normal HR/disciplinary and, if warranted, legal process (unauthorized data disclosure of this scale may itself have criminal dimensions for the individual, independent of your corporate PDPL exposure).
- Use this to trigger a control fix: review who has export/bulk-download rights to customer PII, add data loss prevention (DLP) controls on outbound email for large PII exports, and refresh workforce training on data handling — evidence of a documented root-cause fix matters both for SDAIA's assessment of the incident and for demonstrating "adequate safeguards" going forward.

## Penalty exposure
- Fines up to **SAR 5,000,000 per violation** (doubling for repeat violations) apply to PDPL breaches generally.
- **Criminal exposure up to 2 years' imprisonment** applies specifically to unlawful disclosure of **sensitive data** — get the classification question above resolved with counsel, since it determines whether this provision is in play here; even if national ID isn't classified as "sensitive" under PDPL's specific list, the scale (40,000 records) and nature of the data still drive significant fine exposure and enforcement attention.
- SDAIA's enforcement committees are actively issuing decisions (roughly 48 in the first wave, 2025–26) — this is not a regime that lets incidents like this go unaddressed. Treat prompt, well-documented notification and remediation as materially mitigating in any enforcement review.

## Recommended immediate sequence
1. Contain and preserve evidence (today).
2. Legal counsel engaged now, both for the SDAIA notification and for vendor recovery/legal options.
3. Scope confirmation (data fields, exact count, vendor's current possession/use status).
4. SDAIA notification within the 72-hour window from awareness.
5. Customer notification plan given the risk profile.
6. Root-cause remediation (DLP, access review, training) documented for your regulatory file.

# Unauthorized Disclosure of 40,000 Customer Records — Obligations Under Saudi Law

*Disclaimer: General guidance based on publicly known provisions of the Saudi Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) and related regulations, not legal advice. Given the scale (40,000 individuals) and inclusion of national ID numbers, engage Saudi data protection counsel immediately and in parallel with the steps below.*

## 1. Immediate Framing

This is a personal data breach under the **Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL)** and its Implementing Regulations, regulated by the **Saudi Data & Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA)**. The facts that make this higher-severity than a routine incident:
- **Scale**: 40,000 individuals is a large-scale breach.
- **Data type**: national ID numbers are a unique national identifier tied to a person's legal identity and, combined with names/contact data, create significant identity-theft and fraud risk — regulators and courts will treat this as high-risk/high-harm data.
- **Cause**: an internal employee sent the data to an *external, unauthorized* recipient — this is not a hack, it's an internal control failure (unauthorized processing/disclosure), which raises questions about your access controls, data loss prevention, and processor/vendor management.

## 2. Immediate Response Obligations (Containment)

1. **Contain the breach**: Attempt to recall/delete the email, request written confirmation of deletion and non-use from the external vendor, and consider whether a legal hold or non-disclosure/data-destruction undertaking should be obtained from the vendor in writing.
2. **Preserve evidence**: Retain logs (email metadata, access logs, DLP alerts if any) — you will need this both for your internal investigation and for any SDAIA inquiry.
3. **Suspend the responsible employee's access** pending investigation, consistent with your internal disciplinary policy and Saudi labor law procedures.

## 3. Regulatory Notification Obligations

Under the PDPL Implementing Regulations, controllers must notify the competent authority (SDAIA) of a personal data breach **without undue delay** — the Implementing Regulations set a **72-hour** benchmark from the point the controller becomes aware of an incident that meets the notification threshold (breaches likely to cause harm to the data subject or their data).

- **Notify SDAIA**: Given the volume and sensitivity of the data (national IDs), this breach almost certainly crosses the notification threshold. Prepare a notification describing the nature of the breach, categories and approximate number of individuals/records affected, likely consequences, and measures taken/proposed.
- **Notify affected individuals**: If the breach is likely to result in harm to the data subjects or their data (which is a reasonable conclusion here, given national ID exposure), you are also obligated to notify the affected individuals directly, without undue delay, describing the nature of the incident and recommended protective steps (e.g., watching for identity-theft indicators).
- **Sector regulator notification**: If your company is also regulated by another authority (e.g., SAMA if you handle payments, CST/CITC for telecom-adjacent services, or MoC for consumer protection), check whether that regulator has its own separate breach notification requirement — PDPL notification does not automatically satisfy sector-specific obligations.

## 4. Internal/Contractual Issues to Address

- **Vendor relationship**: If the external vendor was meant to be a legitimate data processor, this incident may also reveal that you lacked (or did not follow) a proper PDPL-compliant Data Processing Agreement — PDPL requires written contractual terms governing any third party's processing of personal data on your behalf, including purpose limitation, security obligations, and data return/destruction at the end of the engagement. If no such agreement existed, or the vendor was not authorized to receive this data at all, this transfer was itself an unauthorized processing/disclosure event independent of any subsequent misuse by the vendor.
- **Access controls**: Investigate why a marketing employee had unrestricted access/export capability to a dataset of 40,000 full customer records including national IDs — this is a strong governance failure indicator (lack of least-privilege access, no DLP controls on outbound email, no approval workflow for bulk data exports) that SDAIA is likely to scrutinize as part of any inquiry into root cause and accountability.
- **HR/disciplinary process**: Handle the employee matter through your internal disciplinary process consistent with the Saudi Labor Law; depending on intent and findings, this could range from formal warning to termination, and in cases involving apparent malicious intent or personal gain, potential referral to the Public Prosecution.

## 5. Potential Penalties and Liability Exposure

- **Administrative fines**: PDPL violations can carry substantial fines (regulations set maximum fine tiers, historically referenced up to several million SAR for serious violations, with the ability to double fines for repeat violations) — the scale and sensitivity here places you at the higher end of regulatory risk.
- **Criminal exposure**: The PDPL includes criminal penalties (including potential imprisonment) specifically for the unlawful disclosure or misuse of sensitive personal data, particularly if disclosure is found to be intentional or for personal benefit or to cause harm — this is a relevant consideration given the employee's role in directly sending the data externally without authorization, even though intent/motive still needs to be established through investigation.
- **Civil liability**: Affected individuals may have a right to compensation for material or moral damage suffered as a result of a PDPL violation; with 40,000 affected individuals, aggregate exposure could be significant if harm materializes (e.g., identity theft, fraud).
- **Reputational and commercial risk**: Regulatory investigation, required corrective action plans, and potential public disclosure obligations can also affect customer trust and B2B relationships.

## 6. Recommended Next Steps (in order)
1. Engage Saudi data protection counsel and, if available, a forensic/incident-response firm today.
2. Complete containment (recall data, secure written vendor confirmation of deletion/non-use).
3. Run a fast but thorough root-cause investigation (how the employee accessed/exported the data, whether DLP/approval controls existed and failed or were absent).
4. Prepare and submit the SDAIA breach notification within the 72-hour benchmark, and prepare individual notifications to the 40,000 affected customers.
5. Review and remediate the underlying access control and data governance gaps (least-privilege access to full PII/national ID datasets, DLP on outbound communications, mandatory approval for bulk exports).
6. Document every step taken (accountability principle) — SDAIA will expect to see a documented incident record and remediation plan, not just the notification itself.
7. Address the employee matter through HR/legal channels in parallel, keeping personnel action separate from (but coordinated with) the regulatory response.

# ISO 27001:2022 vs NCA ECC-2:2024 — Coverage and Remaining Gaps

A couple of confirmations that would sharpen the gap list — I've proceeded on stated assumptions:

- You said "Saudi government subsidiary," so **NCA ECC-2:2024 is mandatory** for you outright (government entities and their subsidiaries are always ECC-covered, no CNI test needed).
- I'm assuming your ISO 27001:2022 certification is current, covers the same organizational/system scope as the ECC assessment will need to cover, and that you haven't yet run a formal ECC self-assessment.
- I'm assuming you also process Saudi residents' personal data (near-universal for any operating entity) and use cloud infrastructure to some degree — both add obligations beyond ECC itself (see matrix).

## Applicability Matrix

| Instrument | Regulator | Applies to you? |
|---|---|---|
| **NCA ECC-2:2024** | NCA | **Yes — mandatory.** Government subsidiaries are always ECC-covered. |
| **NCA CCC** (Cloud Cybersecurity Controls) | NCA | **Yes, if you use cloud** — tenant-side controls, since you're an ECC-covered entity. Confirm your cloud footprint. |
| **NCA DCC-1:2022** (Data Cybersecurity Controls) | NCA | **Likely yes** — data-lifecycle controls for ECC-covered entities. |
| **NCA OTCC-1:2022 / TCC-1:2021 / CSCC-1:2019** | NCA | **Conditional** — only if you operate OT/ICS environments, telework at scale, or critical systems respectively. Flag if any apply; otherwise out of scope here. |
| **Saudi PDPL** | SDAIA | **Yes — mandatory**, independent of ECC, for any personal data you process. |
| **ISO 27001:2022** | (voluntary certification, not a Saudi legal instrument) | Your existing certification — valuable as evidence and control-maturity signal, but it does **not** substitute for NCA's ECC self-assessment/reporting obligation. |

**The core point:** ISO 27001:2022 certification is strong *evidence* for many ECC controls, but it does not satisfy the ECC compliance obligation itself. NCA requires its own self-assessment against ECC's specific control set, submitted through NCA's compliance tool, with NCA audit/on-site assessment rights — a third-party ISO certificate is supporting evidence, not a substitute filing.

## Domain-by-domain coverage estimate

ECC-2:2024 has **4 domains, 28 subdomains, 108 main controls + 92 subcontrols** (control IDs in domain-subdomain-control format, e.g., 1-1-1). I'm citing by domain/subdomain name rather than specific control IDs, since a precise control-ID crosswalk requires the official ECC-2:2024 text and your actual Statement of Applicability — treat the below as a planning-level estimate, not a certified mapping.

| ECC Domain | Roughly maps to (ISO 27001:2022 Annex A) | Coverage from ISO cert | What still needs direct ECC work |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Cybersecurity Governance** — strategy, management commitment, policies, roles, risk management, HR security, awareness, in-project cybersecurity, compliance review | Annex A Organizational controls (A.5) + People controls (A.6) | **Substantial overlap.** ISO's ISMS governance, risk methodology, HR security, and awareness program map closely. | NCA-specific compliance reporting cadence and channel; **Arabic-language governance documentation** where NCA requires it; explicit "in-project cybersecurity" control (security-by-design gates in project management) is more prescriptive under ECC than ISO's general A.8.25/8.26 secure development controls — verify you have a dedicated project-stage-gate process, not just SDLC controls. |
| **2. Cybersecurity Defense** — asset mgmt, identity/access, system/info protection, email, network, mobile, data protection, cryptography, backup, vulnerability/patch mgmt, penetration testing, logging/monitoring, incident & threat mgmt, physical security, web app security | Annex A Technological controls (A.8) + Physical controls (A.7) | **Substantial overlap** — this is ISO 27001:2022's deepest coverage area (asset inventory A.5.9-5.14, access control A.5.15-5.18, cryptography A.8.24, network security A.8.20-8.23, backup A.8.13, vulnerability mgmt A.8.8, logging A.8.15-8.16, incident mgmt A.5.24-5.28, physical A.7, web app security A.8.26). | Verify **frequency and rigor** match ECC's specific expectations (e.g., penetration testing cadence, patch SLAs) — ECC often specifies concrete thresholds where ISO leaves them to risk-based judgment; you'll need to confirm your current SLAs meet ECC's explicit bar, not just "a documented policy exists." Evidence needs to be mapped to NCA's assessment rating scale (implemented / partially implemented / not implemented / N/A with justification). |
| **3. Cybersecurity Resilience** — business continuity aspects of cybersecurity | ISO 27001:2022 A.5.29–5.30 (ICT readiness for business continuity) | **Partial overlap.** ISO 27001:2022 added BC-related controls in the 2022 refresh, but treats resilience as one control area among many. | ECC treats this as a full standalone domain with more depth — you likely need a **dedicated cybersecurity resilience testing and reporting program** (not just a general BCP) to satisfy this domain fully. Gap-assess your current BC/DR testing evidence specifically against ECC's resilience subdomains. |
| **4. Third-Party & Cloud Computing Cybersecurity** — supplier/outsourcing cybersecurity, cloud computing cybersecurity | ISO 27001:2022 A.5.19–5.23 (supplier relationships) | **Partial overlap** on general third-party risk management. | ISO doesn't address **NCA CCC's role-based, cloud-level-tied controls** or **in-Kingdom residency requirements** at all — these are Saudi-specific and need a dedicated build-out: confirm your cloud tenant-side CCC controls, data classification (Top Secret/Secret/Confidential/Public) mapped to the correct cloud level, and residency posture for any cloud-hosted data. Government subsidiary status likely means default-to-in-Kingdom hosting expectations regardless of specific classification. |

## What specifically remains, beyond the domain table

1. **Formal ECC self-assessment and NCA submission** — your ISO audit trail doesn't automatically populate this; you need a control-by-control ECC self-assessment (108 main controls + 92 subcontrols) with evidence mapped to NCA's rating scale, submitted via NCA's compliance tool, and be prepared for NCA audit/on-site assessment.
2. **Arabic-language governance artifacts** where NCA requires them — confirm which policy/procedure documents need Arabic versions for NCA review.
3. **PDPL registration and program**, entirely separate from ECC — SDAIA National Data Governance Platform registration, RoPA, DPO assessment, breach notification procedure (72-hour SDAIA clock). ISO 27001 doesn't cover this at all; it's a parallel legal obligation, not a subset of ECC.
4. **NCA CCC tenant-side controls and cloud residency confirmation** if you use any cloud services — this is the biggest structural gap ISO doesn't touch.
5. **OT/ICS, telework, and critical-systems controls** (OTCC/TCC/CSCC) if any of those environments exist in your operations — these sit outside ECC-2:2024 itself (ICS was moved out of ECC-2 into standalone OTCC-1:2022) and outside ISO 27001 entirely; confirm applicability.
6. **Resilience domain depth** — likely your single biggest content gap versus ISO, since ECC treats cybersecurity resilience as a full domain while ISO 27001:2022 covers it more lightly.

## Recommended next step
Run a formal control-by-control ECC-2:2024 gap assessment using your ISO 27001 Statement of Applicability and audit evidence as the starting evidence base — expect high reuse in Domains 1–2, and dedicated new work in Domains 3–4 plus the PDPL/SDAIA registration track, which sits outside ECC and outside ISO entirely. If you share your current ISO SoA and cloud footprint, I can build the full Requirement/Control ref/Current state/Gap/Evidence needed/Priority table per subdomain.
