Here is the change-management (Domain 2) section of the RCM for the billing system, built to the standard workpaper format — risk statement anchored to misstatement, not generic security language, since that's what auditors expect to see and what actually justifies the control's existence.

| # | Risk | Control objective | Control activity | Type (P/D) | Automation (A/M/ITDM) | Frequency | Owner | Evidence | Test approach | Framework refs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BC-CM-01 | Unauthorized or unapproved changes to billing engine logic (rate rules, revenue recognition parameters, invoice calculation logic) cause misstated revenue | Ensure all changes to production are approved before migration | Change requests for the billing engine require documented business/IT approval in the change management ticketing tool prior to migration to production | P | ITDM (IT-dependent manual — system-enforced ticket gate, manually approved) | Per change (continuous) | Billing Engineering Lead / Change Advisory Board | Change tickets with approval timestamps; CAB minutes; deployment logs | TOD: walkthrough one change end-to-end. TOE: sample 25 changes (daily/frequent-change convention) from the population; trace ticket → approval date/time → migration date; confirm approval precedes migration | AS 2201 (design/operation); COSO Control Activities |
| BC-CM-02 | Changes deployed without adequate testing cause processing errors or incorrect billing/revenue calculations | Ensure changes are tested and results documented before go-live | Test plans and results (including UAT where the change affects billing logic) are completed and attached to the change ticket before migration | P | M | Per change | QA Lead / Billing Product Owner | Test plans, test execution results, UAT sign-off attached to ticket | TOD: walkthrough. TOE: same 25-change sample — inspect test evidence exists, is dated before migration, and covers the change scope | AS 2201; COSO Control Activities |
| BC-CM-03 | Developers can migrate their own code to production, bypassing independent review (self-approval/self-deployment risk) | Segregate development and production-deployment duties | Access to the production deployment/CI-CD pipeline for the billing engine is restricted to a deployment team distinct from developers; developers cannot push directly to production | P | ITDM | Continuous (tested via access review + sample) | DevOps Lead | Pipeline access listings; role/group configuration export; comparison of developer roster to deploy-tool permissions | TOD: walkthrough of pipeline permission model. TOE: obtain full developer population and full deploy-tool access population; test for overlap; for any overlap identified (e.g., small team, tooling merges roles), test the compensating independent review control instead | AS 2201; COSO Control Activities, SoD principle |
| BC-CM-04 | Emergency changes bypass normal approval/testing gates, are made without prior authorization, and are never retrospectively reviewed | Ensure emergency changes follow an expedited but controlled path with after-the-fact review | Emergency changes require expedited authorization (documented, e.g., verbal/Slack approval by on-call lead) at time of change, logged in the emergency change register, and reviewed/approved after the fact by someone independent of the change within a defined window | P/D (hybrid — preventive authorization + detective after-the-fact review) | M | Per emergency change | Engineering Director / Change Manager | Emergency change log; after-the-fact review sign-off | TOD: walkthrough. TOE: sample all emergency changes in the period (full population is typical here given usually low volume); confirm authorization at time of change and completed post-review | AS 2201; COSO Control Activities |
| BC-CM-05 | Configuration and master-data-engine changes (e.g., billing rate tables, tax/rule engine parameters) bypass change control because they're not tracked as "code changes" | Ensure the change population subject to BC-CM-01/02 includes configuration and rules-engine changes, not just application code deployments | Population completeness check: reconcile the change-ticket population against a system-generated deployment/config-change log to confirm no configuration changes occurred outside the ticketed process | D | ITDM | Quarterly (population completeness check convention; more frequent if change volume is high) | Change Manager / Internal Audit liaison | Reconciliation between ticket population and system deployment/config logs; exception listing | TOD: walkthrough of reconciliation method. TOE: sample 2 quarters (quarterly convention) — inspect reconciliation performed, exceptions investigated and resolved | AS 2201; COSO Control Activities, Monitoring |

**How auditors will actually test this section, end to end:**
1. **Population completeness first** — before sampling, auditors (and you, pre-audit) will confirm the change ticket log is the complete population, typically via BC-CM-05's reconciliation against the system's own deployment/config log. A sample drawn from an incomplete population is worthless, and this is consistently one of PCAOB's most-cited findings.
2. **Sample and trace** — using the 25-item convention for a frequently-changing custom system (agree the exact number with your auditor; it's convention, not rule), trace each sampled change from ticket creation through approval, testing evidence, and migration date, confirming approval and testing precede migration (BC-CM-01/02).
3. **SoD test** — full-population comparison of developer access to deploy-tool access (BC-CM-03), not a sample, since it's a design/configuration fact rather than a per-transaction test.
4. **Emergency changes tested separately** — typically full population given lower volume, checking both the at-the-time authorization and the after-the-fact review (BC-CM-04).
5. **Exceptions drive follow-up**, not automatic failure — any exception found (e.g., a change approved after migration) gets root-caused; isolated timing issues with strong testing evidence otherwise may still support operating effectiveness, but a pattern, or one exception combined with a failed SoD test, escalates to a deficiency evaluation.

Note the sample sizes and cadences above are audit convention (daily/frequent≈25, quarterly≈2), not an SEC or PCAOB rule — confirm the exact numbers with your external auditor before finalizing the test plan, and remember this ITGC section only matters insofar as it supports the automated revenue-calculation and invoicing controls the billing engine performs — if a change-management gap is found, evaluate its severity through those downstream revenue controls, not the ITGC failure in isolation.

Below is a working change-management section for an ITGC risk and control matrix (RCM) for a billing system, covering risk, control objective, control activity, control owner, frequency, and the typical audit test of controls. Adjust owners/tools to your environment.

Control Objective: Changes to the billing system (application code, configurations, interfaces, and underlying database/infrastructure) are authorized, tested, and approved before being moved into production, so that unauthorized or erroneous changes do not compromise the completeness, accuracy, or validity of billing and revenue data.

Risk being addressed: Unauthorized, untested, or improperly approved changes to the billing engine could result in incorrect invoice calculation, revenue misstatement, broken interfaces to the GL/ERP, or a change that intentionally or unintentionally circumvents application controls (e.g., pricing logic, discount limits, revenue recognition rules).

Key controls typically included:

1. Change request and authorization control.
Control activity: All changes to the billing system (code, configuration, master data rules, interface logic) must be logged as a formal change request/ticket, including business justification, and approved by a designated change approver (e.g., engineering lead or change advisory board) before development begins.
Control owner: Engineering manager / Change Advisory Board (CAB).
Frequency: Per change (continuous/ongoing).
Audit test approach: Auditors will select a sample of changes deployed during the period from the change log/ticketing system (e.g., Jira, ServiceNow), and for each sampled change, inspect evidence that a ticket exists, that it was approved prior to development or deployment, and that the approver had appropriate authority and was independent of the developer (segregation of duties).

2. System/user acceptance testing control.
Control activity: All changes are tested in a non-production environment (dev/QA/UAT) before deployment, with documented test cases, test results, and business/QA sign-off, commensurate with the risk of the change.
Control owner: QA lead / Business process owner (for UAT sign-off).
Frequency: Per change.
Audit test approach: For the same sample, inspect test plans/scripts, evidence of test execution (e.g., screenshots, test management tool records), and a documented sign-off/approval indicating the change met acceptance criteria before promotion.

3. Segregation of duties in the deployment pipeline.
Control activity: Developers do not have the ability to independently move their own code into the production billing environment; a separate release/deployment function (or automated CI/CD pipeline with approval gates) performs the production deployment, and access to promote code to production is restricted to authorized personnel who are not the code's author.
Control owner: DevOps/Release management.
Frequency: Continuous (enforced via access controls and pipeline configuration); reviewed periodically.
Audit test approach: Review access listings for who can deploy to production, confirm developers lack direct production deployment rights (or that compensating peer-review/approval gates exist in the CI/CD tool), and trace a sample of deployments to confirm the deployer was different from (or independently approved by someone other than) the developer.

4. Change approval prior to production migration (go/no-go).
Control activity: A final approval is obtained and documented immediately prior to production release, confirming testing is complete, business sign-off obtained, and rollback plan exists.
Control owner: Release manager / CAB.
Frequency: Per change/release.
Audit test approach: Inspect release records or deployment logs for the sampled changes and confirm a final approval artifact (e.g., CAB minutes, approval workflow in the ticketing tool) exists dated on or before the production deployment date/timestamp.

5. Emergency change control.
Control activity: Emergency/urgent changes follow an expedited but still-controlled process: post-implementation review and retroactive approval within a defined window (e.g., 24-48 hours), with documented justification for bypassing standard testing/approval steps.
Control owner: Engineering manager / IT management.
Frequency: Per emergency change (as needed).
Audit test approach: Obtain the population of emergency changes for the period, select a sample, and verify retroactive approval and documented justification exist within the policy-defined window; assess whether emergency changes were appropriately rare and not used to circumvent normal controls.

6. Change management for interfaces and data feeds.
Control activity: Changes to interfaces between the billing system and downstream systems (GL/ERP, data warehouse) follow the same authorization/testing/approval process, with specific reconciliation or parallel-run testing to confirm data integrity across the interface before go-live.
Control owner: Integration/engineering lead.
Frequency: Per interface change.
Audit test approach: For sampled interface changes, inspect reconciliation/parallel-testing evidence in addition to standard change documentation.

7. Periodic review of the change management policy and access to production.
Control activity: IT management periodically reviews the change management policy for continued adequacy and reviews the list of personnel with production access/deployment rights to confirm it remains appropriate.
Control owner: IT/Engineering leadership.
Frequency: Annually, or upon significant process change.
Audit test approach: Inspect the current policy document, evidence of periodic review/approval (e.g., sign-off date), and the most recent production access review.

Sampling and evidence notes for auditors: Expect auditors to request the full population of changes for the audit period (typically pulled directly from the ticketing/CI-CD system, not a manually curated list), select samples based on risk and population size (often 25-40 for operating effectiveness over a full year, fewer for design/implementation-only testing), and expect complete documentary trails (ticket, approval timestamps, test evidence, deployment logs) rather than verbal confirmation. Gaps commonly cited in this area include: missing evidence of testing for "minor" changes, developers with residual production access, inconsistent use of the emergency change process for what should be standard changes, and undocumented configuration-only changes (e.g., pricing table updates) that are treated as "not code changes" and therefore skip the control process entirely — this last one is a frequent audit finding for billing systems specifically, since pricing/discount configuration changes can affect revenue just as much as code changes.
Prompt: Design our annual SOX ITGC calendar. We're a calendar-year accelerated filer and remediation always surprises us in Q4.
With Skill
⭐⭐⭐⭐ 4/5 assertions passed (80%)
✅Lays out a quarterly rhythm: Q1 scoping refresh/RCM updates, Q2 walkthroughs + interim testing, Q3 second testing wave + deficiency triage while remediation windows remain, Q4 roll-forward/update testing, remediation validation, aggregation analysis, management's 404(a) conclusion
✅Places user access reviews quarterly and terminations/privileged-access checks as continuous — the classic late-surprise sources
✅Builds remediation timing logic: controls fixed late can't demonstrate sufficient operating history — deficiencies found in Q3 or earlier leave a re-test window; that's why triage belongs mid-year
❌Includes deficiency aggregation and severity classification (AS 2201/Reg S-X ladder) ahead of the year-end conclusion, with audit-committee reporting for significant deficiencies
✅References current context accurately where used: COSO 2013 as the framework, PCAOB inspection focus on ICFR, ~8% of recent annual reports disclosing material weaknesses with IT/access among top themes
The Q4 remediation surprise is almost always a sequencing problem, not a testing-effort problem: teams find deficiencies late enough that there's no operating window left to prove the fix before year-end. The fix is to build the calendar backward from year-end re-testing requirements, not forward from January. Here's a full-year design for a calendar-year accelerated filer.

**Governing principle (state this up front and keep it visible all year):** a control fixed in December cannot demonstrate operation for the period — a quarterly control needs at least one clean quarterly occurrence after remediation, and a daily control commonly needs a fresh sample (25-convention) of clean operation before you can conclude it's operating effectively by year-end. Every date below is chosen to leave that window open.

**Q1 (Jan–Mar): Scope and refresh, don't wait to test.**
- Refresh the scoping memo: confirm significant accounts, processes, and in-scope systems/layers haven't shifted (new systems, M&A, material process change).
- Update RCMs for any system or process changes from the prior year.
- Run User Access Review (UAR) cycle 1 for all in-scope systems.
- Kick off TOD (design/walkthrough) for any new or redesigned controls immediately — don't defer walkthroughs to Q2 if a control changed.
- Continuous, not quarterly: termination deprovisioning and privileged access — review monthly at minimum; these are your highest-frequency source of late surprises (see: prior findings on terminated users retaining access for months).

**Q2 (Apr–Jun): First substantive testing wave.**
- TOD walkthroughs for all in-scope controls not already covered in Q1.
- Interim TOE wave 1 — begin operating-effectiveness testing on your annual/quarterly-frequency controls now, not in Q4, since those have few occurrences per year and you need to see them fail (if they will) with time to fix.
- UAR cycle 2.
- **Deficiency triage begins here, not Q3** — any control failure surfaced in Q1/Q2 testing gets root-caused and moved into remediation design immediately. This is the single highest-leverage change from your current process: treat Q2 findings as needing to be *fixed and re-tested by Q4*, and work backward from that.

**Q3 (Jul–Sep): Interim TOE wave 2 and the last real remediation window.**
- Interim TOE wave 2, covering remaining populations and any controls not fully tested in Q2.
- UAR cycle 3.
- Deficiency triage continues, but treat Q3 as the *last quarter where a newly designed remediation can still generate a clean quarterly operating occurrence before year-end.* If a quarterly control needs to prove one clean cycle post-remediation, the redesign has to be live by the start of Q3 at the latest — not discovered in Q3.
- Run a **mid-year aggregation check**: don't wait until Q4 to see how individual deficiencies might combine against the same significant account/assertion. Aggregation can turn three "minor" items into a significant deficiency or worse, and you want that visibility while there's still time to remediate, not as a year-end surprise.

**Q4 (Oct–Dec): Roll-forward, validate, conclude — not discover.**
- Roll-forward testing/update walkthroughs to year-end for any controls only tested at interim.
- **Remediation validation**, not remediation design: by Q4, every deficiency should already have a redesigned control in place with at least the minimum required operating history behind it (one clean quarter for quarterly controls; a fresh clean sample for daily/frequent controls). Q4 activity is testing that evidence, not scrambling to fix root causes.
- Final aggregation analysis across all deficiencies identified all year, evaluated against significant accounts/assertions.
- UAR cycle 4.
- Management's 404(a) conclusion, drafted with enough lead time for audit committee review before the 10-K deadline.
- Terminations and privileged access: same continuous cadence as all year — do not let this lapse into a year-end-only check; it's explicitly the highest-risk area for late, ugly surprises (unbounded-magnitude access exposure is exactly the fact pattern that drives material weakness findings).

**The structural change that actually solves your Q4 problem:** move deficiency *identification* earlier (Q2 interim testing, not Q3/Q4) so that remediation *design and implementation* happens in Q2–Q3, leaving Q3–Q4 purely for re-testing and validation. If you're currently identifying issues in Q4 UAR or year-end testing, you've structurally guaranteed you can't prove a clean operating period before your 404(a) conclusion — that's a timing problem no amount of Q4 effort fixes.

**Two calendar-specific flags for your situation:**
- As an accelerated filer, confirm your 404(b) auditor attestation status hasn't changed (it applies unless you're also an EGC) — this affects how much of the above your external auditor will independently re-perform versus rely on.
- Watch the SEC's May 19, 2026 proposal (raising large-accelerated threshold to $2B float, broader 404(b) exemptions, ~5-year IPO on-ramp) — it's not final and shouldn't change this year's calendar, but revisit before building next year's.

Document this calendar with explicit named owners and dates per quarter (not just "Q2: testing") — the surprises tend to hide in ambiguous ownership as much as in the schedule itself.

❌Places user access reviews quarterly and terminations/privileged-access checks as continuous — the classic late-surprise sources

Here's an annual SOX ITGC calendar for a calendar-year accelerated filer, structured to spread testing across the year and specifically pull remediation activity forward so it doesn't ambush you in Q4. The core idea: front-load control testing and walkthroughs into Q1-Q2, use Q3 as your "last clean window" to fix anything found, and reserve Q4 for roll-forward/confirmation work only — not first-time remediation.

Q1 (January-March):
- Finalize prior-year SOX assessment wrap-up: close out any remaining prior-year deficiencies, confirm remediation was validated, and brief the audit committee on final status alongside the 10-K filing.
- Refresh the risk assessment and scoping: update significant accounts, in-scope systems/processes, and the RCM for any changes (new systems, M&A, process changes, new revenue streams) from the prior year.
- Update process narratives and control matrices for any changes identified in scoping.
- Kick off Q1 walkthroughs for key ITGC and process-level controls (access, change management, computer operations) to confirm design still matches practice after any changes.
- Begin first-round interim testing of controls that operate frequently (e.g., monthly access reviews, daily job monitoring) so you have multiple testing touchpoints across the year, not just one at year-end.
- Align with external auditors on the current-year audit plan, scoping, materiality, and reliance strategy (including any planned reliance on your internal testing).

Q2 (April-June):
- Continue interim testing: this is typically your heaviest internal testing window for ITGC operating effectiveness — access provisioning/deprovisioning samples, change management samples, backup/job monitoring, and quarterly user access reviews (Q1 and Q2 UARs should both be tested by now).
- Conduct the mid-year privileged/user access review with particular attention to terminated employees and segregation-of-duties conflicts; this is the review most likely to catch the kind of stale-account issue that otherwise surfaces late in the year.
- Track and log all deficiencies found so far in a live issues log (severity, root cause, owner, target remediation date) rather than waiting to compile this at year-end.
- Auditor interim fieldwork/testing typically occurs in this window — coordinate PBC (prepared-by-client) requests and evidence delivery to avoid a bottleneck later.
- Re-assess filer status inputs (float, revenue) if relevant to your EGC/accelerated filer classification.

Q3 (July-September):
- This is your "remediation deadline" quarter, not a discovery quarter. Any deficiency identified in Q1/Q2 testing should be substantially remediated and retested by the end of Q3, so you go into Q4 with a clean population.
- Perform Q3 user access reviews and any other quarterly-frequency controls; these are your last chance to catch and fix an issue with enough runway to demonstrate the control operating effectively again before year-end.
- Conduct a formal mid-year deficiency evaluation session with management/disclosure committee: review the issues log, classify severity, and confirm nothing is trending toward a significant deficiency or material weakness without a remediation plan in motion.
- Update management's 404(a) assessment working papers with results to date; flag any area needing incremental testing in Q4.
- If new systems or major changes are planned for Q4 or Q1 next year (common cause of late-year surprises), pull related control design work and testing forward into Q3 rather than letting it land in the year-end crunch.

Q4 (October-December):
- Perform roll-forward testing only for controls tested earlier in the year (confirming no changes since interim testing, per PCAOB guidance on using interim testing with a roll-forward period) — this should be light-touch, not first-time testing.
- Complete year-end procedures for controls that only operate annually (e.g., annual risk assessment sign-off, annual DR/BCP test, annual vendor SOC report review and CUEC mapping).
- Finalize the Q4 user access review and any final segregation-of-duties analysis, with enough buffer (target completion by early-to-mid December) to remediate anything found before year-end close — this is the single biggest lever for stopping Q4 surprises, since most "surprise" findings are UAR-related and discovered too close to the 10-K filing date.
- Close the annual issues log: finalize severity conclusions on all deficiencies, confirm remediation and retesting evidence for anything found during the year, and prepare the management representation letter content.
- Hold final auditor closing meetings and obtain their preliminary view on ICFR effectiveness before finalizing management's 404(a) conclusion.
- Present the annual ICFR effectiveness conclusion, deficiency summary, and remediation status to the audit committee ahead of the 10-K filing.

Cross-cutting recommendations to prevent Q4 surprises specifically:
- Move your control testing cadence to quarterly (not annual) for anything auditors will sample across the full year, so no single quarter carries all the testing risk.
- Set an internal policy that any deficiency identified after October 31 triggers an automatic escalation to the disclosure committee, since there's little runway left to remediate and retest before year-end.
- Track "days to remediate" as a metric across the issues log — if your average remediation time is, say, 45 days, then any Q3 deficiency found after mid-November effectively can't be fully remediated and retested before year-end, which tells you exactly how early your Q3 testing needs to finish.
- Build a standing quarterly "SOX steering committee" checkpoint (IT, finance, internal audit, external audit liaison) so issues surface and get owners assigned continuously, rather than being aggregated for the first time at year-end.
